question.html:
Question 11
?

A meteorologist measured two particular features, x1 and x2, at various locations throughout California. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular location. The first and second principal components of the data are approximately v1≈[0.6670.745],v2≈[−0.7450.667].

By combining the two measured features linearly, the meteorologist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?

a
 −0.745x1+0.667x2
b
0.667x1+0.745x2
c
 0.667x1−0.745x2
d
0.667(x1+x2)
e
0.745x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the first principal component of the data.

Let

V=[||v1v2||]=[0.667−0.7450.7450.667]

be the matrix of principal components.

Then, applying the change of variables Y=XV, we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1 and y2 are uncorrelated), and

  • the features y1 and y2 are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in y1).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation x=[x1x2], we get

[y1y2]=[x1x2]V=[x1x2][0.667−0.7450.7450.667]=[0.667x1+0.745x2−0.745x1+0.667x2].

As a result, we have that y1=0.667x1+0.745x2 will contain most of the variance of the data.

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

y1=0.667x1+0.745x2.

solution.reasoning: Project each observation onto the first principal component to retain maximum variance: y_1 = [x_1,x_2]v_1 = 0.667x_1 + 0.745x_2. This is option b. The supplied worked example supports this method but does not capture Math Academy's answer to the current question.

Question 11
?

A meteorologist measured two particular features, x1 and x2, at various locations throughout California. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular location. The first and second principal components of the data are approximately v1≈[0.6670.745],v2≈[−0.7450.667].

By combining the two measured features linearly, the meteorologist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?

a
 −0.745x1+0.667x2
b
0.667x1+0.745x2
c
 0.667x1−0.745x2
d
0.667(x1+x2)
e
0.745x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the first principal component of the data.

Let

V=[||v1v2||]=[0.667−0.7450.7450.667]

be the matrix of principal components.

Then, applying the change of variables Y=XV, we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1 and y2 are uncorrelated), and

  • the features y1 and y2 are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in y1).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation x=[x1x2], we get

[y1y2]=[x1x2]V=[x1x2][0.667−0.7450.7450.667]=[0.667x1+0.745x2−0.745x1+0.667x2].

As a result, we have that y1=0.667x1+0.745x2 will contain most of the variance of the data.

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

y1=0.667x1+0.745x2.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198769/assets/171a9c86bf510c2ee5b65325d6f8939c65b5118286057934f91a053f75faf82f.png)

  

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.555 & 0.832 \\ 0.832 & 0.555\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-0.555 & 0.832 \\ 0.832 & 0.555\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-0.555{x}_{1}+0.832{x}_{2} & 0.832{x}_{1}+0.555{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=-0.555{x}_{1}+0.832{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=-0.555{x}_{1}+0.832{x}_{2}.
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
A physicist measured two particular features, ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ for each oscillation produced when a mass hanging on a spring is displaced and then released. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular oscillation. 
The first and second principal components of the data are approximately

$$
{v}_{1}≈[\begin{aligned}0.456 \\ 0.890\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}≈[\begin{aligned}0.890 \\ -0.456\end{aligned}].
$$

By combining the two measured features linearly, the physicist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?
question.worked_solution:
Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198769/assets/f0f0623703d1a3767a7c3efd275e977c6933465faeb761991f00da705bac4a2c.png)

 

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.456 & 0.890 \\ 0.890 & -0.456\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.456 & 0.890 \\ 0.890 & -0.456\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2} & 0.890{x}_{1}-0.456{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data.

$$
{y}_{1}=0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2}.

question.html:
Question 13
?

A physicist measured two particular features, x1 and x2, for each oscillation produced when a mass hanging on a spring is displaced and then released. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular oscillation. The first and second principal components of the data are approximately v1≈[0.4560.890],v2≈[0.890−0.456].

By combining the two measured features linearly, the physicist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?

a
0.890x1−0.456x2
b
0.456x1+0.890x2
c
 0.890x2
d
0.456(x1+x2)
e
 0.456x1−0.890x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the first principal component of the data.

Let

V=[||v1v2||]=[0.4560.8900.890−0.456]

be the matrix of principal components.

Then, applying the change of variables Y=XV, we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1 and y2 are uncorrelated), and

  • the features y1 and y2 are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in y1).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation x=[x1x2], we get

[y1y2]=[x1x2]V=[x1x2][0.4560.8900.890−0.456]=[0.456x1+0.890x20.890x1−0.456x2].

As a result, we have that y1=0.456x1+0.890x2 will contain most of the variance of the data.

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

y1=0.456x1+0.890x2.

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198769/assets/f0f0623703d1a3767a7c3efd275e977c6933465faeb761991f00da705bac4a2c.png)

 

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.456 & 0.890 \\ 0.890 & -0.456\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.456 & 0.890 \\ 0.890 & -0.456\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2} & 0.890{x}_{1}-0.456{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2}.
$$

question.html:
Question 13
?

A physicist measured two particular features, x1 and x2, for each oscillation produced when a mass hanging on a spring is displaced and then released. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular oscillation. The first and second principal components of the data are approximately v1≈[0.4560.890],v2≈[0.890−0.456].

By combining the two measured features linearly, the physicist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?

a
0.890x1−0.456x2
b
0.456x1+0.890x2
c
 0.890x2
d
0.456(x1+x2)
e
 0.456x1−0.890x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the first principal component of the data.

Let

V=[||v1v2||]=[0.4560.8900.890−0.456]

be the matrix of principal components.

Then, applying the change of variables Y=XV, we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1 and y2 are uncorrelated), and

  • the features y1 and y2 are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in y1).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation x=[x1x2], we get

[y1y2]=[x1x2]V=[x1x2][0.4560.8900.890−0.456]=[0.456x1+0.890x20.890x1−0.456x2].

As a result, we have that y1=0.456x1+0.890x2 will contain most of the variance of the data.

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

y1=0.456x1+0.890x2.
question.knowledge_point: Representing Principal Components as Linear Combinations

solution.reasoning: Projecting onto the given first principal component retains maximum variance: y_1 = [x_1,x_2]v_1 = 0.456x_1 + 0.890x_2. This matches option b. The supplied worked example supports the method but does not establish Math Academy's answer for this question.

feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.problem:
A physicist measured two particular features, ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ for each oscillation produced when a mass hanging on a spring is displaced and then released. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular oscillation. 
The first and second principal components of the data are approximately

$$
{v}_{1}≈[\begin{aligned}0.456 \\ 0.890\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}≈[\begin{aligned}0.890 \\ -0.456\end{aligned}].
$$

By combining the two measured features linearly, the physicist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198769/assets/f0f0623703d1a3767a7c3efd275e977c6933465faeb761991f00da705bac4a2c.png)

 

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.456 & 0.890 \\ 0.890 & -0.456\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.456 & 0.890 \\ 0.890 & -0.456\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2} & 0.890{x}_{1}-0.456{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=0.456{x}_{1}+0.890{x}_{2}.
$$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem:
A neuroscientist measured two specific features, ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ for each brain image of a group of patients he is studying. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular brain image. 
The first and second principal components of the data are approximately

$$
{v}_{1}≈[\begin{aligned}-0.707 \\ -0.707\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}≈[\begin{aligned}-0.707 \\ 0.707\end{aligned}].
$$

By combining the two measured features linearly, the neuroscientist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?
question.worked_solution:
Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198769/assets/70a37afaaad54e3f384ad446ab2cf57bc0f21ffa8f6986f01841d9f4041f531c.png)

  

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.707 & -0.707 \\ -0.707 & 0.707\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-0.707 & -0.707 \\ -0.707 & 0.707\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-0.707{x}_{1}-0.707{x}_{2} & -0.707{x}_{1}+0.707{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=-0.707{x}_{1}-0.707{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=-0.707{x}_{1}-0.707{x}_{2}.
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

A neuroscientist measured two specific features, x1 and x2, for each brain image of a group of patients he is studying. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular brain image. The first and second principal components of the data are approximately v1≈[−0.707−0.707],v2≈[−0.7070.707].

By combining the two measured features linearly, the neuroscientist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?

a
−0.707x1+0.707x2
b
 0.707(x1+x2)
c
 −0.707x2
d
0.707x1−0.707x2
e
 −0.707x1−0.707x2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the first principal component of the data.

Let

V=[||v1v2||]=[−0.707−0.707−0.7070.707]

be the matrix of principal components.

Then, applying the change of variables Y=XV, we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1 and y2 are uncorrelated), and

  • the features y1 and y2 are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in y1).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation x=[x1x2], we get

[y1y2]=[x1x2]V=[x1x2][−0.707−0.707−0.7070.707]=[−0.707x1−0.707x2−0.707x1+0.707x2].

As a result, we have that y1=−0.707x1−0.707x2 will contain most of the variance of the data.

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

y1=−0.707x1−0.707x2.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198769/assets/70a37afaaad54e3f384ad446ab2cf57bc0f21ffa8f6986f01841d9f4041f531c.png)

  

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.707 & -0.707 \\ -0.707 & 0.707\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-0.707 & -0.707 \\ -0.707 & 0.707\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-0.707{x}_{1}-0.707{x}_{2} & -0.707{x}_{1}+0.707{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=-0.707{x}_{1}-0.707{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=-0.707{x}_{1}-0.707{x}_{2}.
$$

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198769/assets/70a37afaaad54e3f384ad446ab2cf57bc0f21ffa8f6986f01841d9f4041f531c.png)

  

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.707 & -0.707 \\ -0.707 & 0.707\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-0.707 & -0.707 \\ -0.707 & 0.707\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-0.707{x}_{1}-0.707{x}_{2} & -0.707{x}_{1}+0.707{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=-0.707{x}_{1}-0.707{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=-0.707{x}_{1}-0.707{x}_{2}.
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

A neuroscientist measured two specific features, x1 and x2, for each brain image of a group of patients he is studying. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular brain image. The first and second principal components of the data are approximately v1≈[−0.707−0.707],v2≈[−0.7070.707].

By combining the two measured features linearly, the neuroscientist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?

a
−0.707x1+0.707x2
b
 0.707(x1+x2)
c
 −0.707x2
d
0.707x1−0.707x2
e
 −0.707x1−0.707x2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the first principal component of the data.

Let

V=[||v1v2||]=[−0.707−0.707−0.7070.707]

be the matrix of principal components.

Then, applying the change of variables Y=XV, we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1 and y2 are uncorrelated), and

  • the features y1 and y2 are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in y1).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation x=[x1x2], we get

[y1y2]=[x1x2]V=[x1x2][−0.707−0.707−0.7070.707]=[−0.707x1−0.707x2−0.707x1+0.707x2].

As a result, we have that y1=−0.707x1−0.707x2 will contain most of the variance of the data.

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

y1=−0.707x1−0.707x2.
question.knowledge_point: Representing Principal Components as Linear Combinations

solution.reasoning: Projection onto the given first principal component gives -0.707x_1-0.707x_2, option e. Option b is its negative and preserves exactly the same variance, since Var(-Y)=Var(Y), so both b and e are mathematically valid. Choose e to match the supplied vector's sign. No current Math Academy answer or grade is captured; the worked example concerns different coefficients.

Question 14
?

A neuroscientist measured two specific features, x1 and x2, for each brain image of a group of patients he is studying. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular brain image. The first and second principal components of the data are approximately v1≈[−0.707−0.707],v2≈[−0.7070.707].

By combining the two measured features linearly, the neuroscientist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?

a
−0.707x1+0.707x2
b
 0.707(x1+x2)
c
 −0.707x2
d
0.707x1−0.707x2
e
 −0.707x1−0.707x2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the first principal component of the data.

Let

V=[||v1v2||]=[−0.707−0.707−0.7070.707]

be the matrix of principal components.

Then, applying the change of variables Y=XV, we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1 and y2 are uncorrelated), and

  • the features y1 and y2 are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in y1).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation x=[x1x2], we get

[y1y2]=[x1x2]V=[x1x2][−0.707−0.707−0.7070.707]=[−0.707x1−0.707x2−0.707x1+0.707x2].

As a result, we have that y1=−0.707x1−0.707x2 will contain most of the variance of the data.

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

y1=−0.707x1−0.707x2.

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
An engineer measured two particular features, ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ for each road bridge in a city. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular bridge. 
The first and second principal components of the data are approximately

$$
{v}_{1}≈[\begin{aligned}0.669 \\ 0.743\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}≈[\begin{aligned}0.743 \\ -0.669\end{aligned}].
$$

By combining the two measured features linearly, the engineer wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?
question.worked_solution:
Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198769/assets/c47327219f03934832e62176db1441a94d9a78edda2f0d398a63b2942ec6a845.png)

  

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.669 & 0.743 \\ 0.743 & -0.669\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.669 & 0.743 \\ 0.743 & -0.669\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.669{x}_{1}+0.743{x}_{2} & 0.743{x}_{1}-0.669{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=0.669{x}_{1}+0.743{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=0.669{x}_{1}+0.743{x}_{2}.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 15
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Representing Principal Components as Linear Combinations
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198769/assets/c47327219f03934832e62176db1441a94d9a78edda2f0d398a63b2942ec6a845.png)

  

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.669 & 0.743 \\ 0.743 & -0.669\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.669 & 0.743 \\ 0.743 & -0.669\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.669{x}_{1}+0.743{x}_{2} & 0.743{x}_{1}-0.669{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=0.669{x}_{1}+0.743{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=0.669{x}_{1}+0.743{x}_{2}.
$$

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
An engineer measured two particular features, ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ for each road bridge in a city. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular bridge. 
The first and second principal components of the data are approximately

$$
{v}_{1}≈[\begin{aligned}0.669 \\ 0.743\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}≈[\begin{aligned}0.743 \\ -0.669\end{aligned}].
$$

By combining the two measured features linearly, the engineer wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.669 & 0.743 \\ 0.743 & -0.669\end{aligned}]
$$

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.669 & 0.743 \\ 0.743 & -0.669\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.669{x}_{1}+0.743{x}_{2} & 0.743{x}_{1}-0.669{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=0.669{x}_{1}+0.743{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data.

question.html:
Question 15
?

An engineer measured two particular features, x1 and x2, for each road bridge in a city. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular bridge. The first and second principal components of the data are approximately v1≈[0.6690.743],v2≈[0.743−0.669].

By combining the two measured features linearly, the engineer wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?

a
 0.669x1+0.743x2
b
 0.743x2
c
 0.669(x1+x2)
d
 0.669x1−0.743x2
e
 0.743x1−0.669x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the first principal component of the data.

Let

V=[||v1v2||]=[0.6690.7430.743−0.669]

be the matrix of principal components.

Then, applying the change of variables Y=XV, we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1 and y2 are uncorrelated), and

  • the features y1 and y2 are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in y1).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation x=[x1x2], we get

[y1y2]=[x1x2]V=[x1x2][0.6690.7430.743−0.669]=[0.669x1+0.743x20.743x1−0.669x2].

As a result, we have that y1=0.669x1+0.743x2 will contain most of the variance of the data.

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

y1=0.669x1+0.743x2.

solution.reasoning: Projection onto the given first principal component retains maximum variance: y_1 = [x_1,x_2]v_1 = 0.669x_1 + 0.743x_2. This matches option a. The supplied worked example supports the method but does not capture Math Academy's answer to this question.

By combining the two measured features linearly, the engineer wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198769/assets/c47327219f03934832e62176db1441a94d9a78edda2f0d398a63b2942ec6a845.png)

  

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.669 & 0.743 \\ 0.743 & -0.669\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.669 & 0.743 \\ 0.743 & -0.669\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.669{x}_{1}+0.743{x}_{2} & 0.743{x}_{1}-0.669{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=0.669{x}_{1}+0.743{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=0.669{x}_{1}+0.743{x}_{2}.
$$

feedback.html:
Question 15
?

An engineer measured two particular features, x1 and x2, for each road bridge in a city. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular bridge. The first and second principal components of the data are approximately v1≈[0.6690.743],v2≈[0.743−0.669].

By combining the two measured features linearly, the engineer wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?

a
 0.669x1+0.743x2
b
 0.743x2
c
 0.669(x1+x2)
d
 0.669x1−0.743x2
e
 0.743x1−0.669x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the first principal component of the data.

Let

V=[||v1v2||]=[0.6690.7430.743−0.669]

be the matrix of principal components.

Then, applying the change of variables Y=XV, we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1 and y2 are uncorrelated), and

  • the features y1 and y2 are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in y1).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation x=[x1x2], we get

[y1y2]=[x1x2]V=[x1x2][0.6690.7430.743−0.669]=[0.669x1+0.743x20.743x1−0.669x2].

As a result, we have that y1=0.669x1+0.743x2 will contain most of the variance of the data.

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

y1=0.669x1+0.743x2.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Are Attained on the Unit Sphere
questions.raw_html:
1.Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Are Attained on the Unit Sphere?

The minimum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=−x12−x22+2x32+2x1x2, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to −2. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

M

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.raw_html:
2.Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Are Attained on the Unit Sphere?

The minimum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=7x12+8x22+5x32−4x2x3, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to 4. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: The maximum  value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum  is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

3.Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Are Attained on the Unit Sphere?

The maximum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+x22+x32−6x1x2, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to 4. Which of the following is a vector x at which the maximum is attained?

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: The minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}]+72[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.raw_html:
5.Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Is Attained Over an Ellipse?

The minimum value of Q(x)=4x12−36x1x2+9x22, when 4x12+9x22=36, is −72. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

H

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 1
?

The minimum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=−x12−x22+2x32+2x1x2, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to −2. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
[110]
b
12[−110]
c
[001]
d
12[110]
e
[100]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[−1101−10002]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=−2:

A−(−2)I=[−1101−10002]−(−2)[100010001]=[110110004]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[−110].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umin=v‖v‖=12[−110].

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 2
?

The minimum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=7x12+8x22+5x32−4x2x3, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to 4. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
13[111]
b
12[122]
c
12[01−1]
d
15[012]
e
12[011]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[70008−20−25]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=4:

A−4I=[70008−20−25]−4[100010001]=[30004−20−21]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[012].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=5, we get

umin=v‖v‖=15[012].

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

The maximum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+x22+x32−6x1x2, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to 4. Which of the following is a vector x at which the maximum is attained?

a
12[101]
b
12[110]
c
12[−110]
d
12[−101]
e
12[011]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1−30−310001]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=4:

A−4I=[1−30−310001]−4[100010001]=[−3−30−3−3000−3]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[−110].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umax=v‖v‖=12[−110].

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4

question.html:
Question 4
?

The maximum value of Q(x)=x12+16x1x2+4x22, when x12+4x22=4, is 20. Which of the following is a vector x at which the maximum is attained?

a
110[13]
b
15[−21]
c
110[−31]
d
12[1−1]
e
12[21]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1884]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

x1222+x2212=1

This is an ellipse with semiaxes a=2 (along the x1-axis) and b=1 (along the x2-axis). If we introduce new variables

y1=x12 and y2=x2,

the equation of the ellipse will transform into y12+y22=1 or ‖y‖=1.

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

P=[2001],

we obtain that x=Py. Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

Q(x)=xTAx=(Py)TA(Py)=yT(PTAP)y=Q′(y).

As a result, since PT=P, the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

B=PTAP=PAP=[2001][1884][2001]=[21684][2001]=[416164].

Now, we maximize Q′(y) when ‖y‖=1, as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is 20, we have

max{Q′(y)|‖y‖=1}=λmax=20.

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmax=20:

B−20I=[416164]−20[1001]=[−161616−16] Seeking a non-zero solution of (B−20I)y=0 gives the eigenvector v=[11]. Dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umax=v‖v‖=12[11].

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

xmax=Pumax=[2001]⋅12[11]=12[21]

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}]+72[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

The minimum value of Q(x)=4x12−36x1x2+9x22, when 4x12+9x22=36, is −72. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
15[−23]
b
15[−12]
c
12[32]
d
110[21]
e
15[12]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[4−18−189]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

x1232+x2222=1

This is an ellipse with semiaxes a=3 (along the x1-axis) and b=2 (along the x2-axis). If we introduce new variables

y1=x13 and y2=x22,

the equation of the ellipse will transform into y12+y22=1 or ‖y‖=1.

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

P=[3002],

we obtain that x=Py. Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

Q(x)=xTAx=(Py)TA(Py)=yT(PTAP)y=Q′(y).

As a result, since PT=P, the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

B=PTAP=PAP=[3002][4−18−189][3002]=[12−54−3618][3002]=[36−108−10836].

Now, we minimize Q′(y) when ‖y‖=1, as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is −72, we have

min{Q′(y)|‖y‖=1}=λmin=−72.

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=−72:

B−(−72)I=[36−108−10836]+72[1001]=[108−108−108108] Seeking a non-zero solution of (B−(−72)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[11]. Dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umin=v‖v‖=12[11].

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

xmin=Pumin=[3002]⋅12[11]=12[32]

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
question.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 1
?

The minimum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=−x12−x22+2x32+2x1x2, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to −2. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
[110]
b
12[−110]
c
[001]
d
12[110]
e
[100]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[−1101−10002]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=−2:

A−(−2)I=[−1101−10002]−(−2)[100010001]=[110110004]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[−110].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umin=v‖v‖=12[−110].

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The minimum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=−x12−x22+2x32+2x1x2, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to −2. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
[110]
b
12[−110]
c
[001]
d
12[110]
e
[100]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[−1101−10002]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=−2:

A−(−2)I=[−1101−10002]−(−2)[100010001]=[110110004]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[−110].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umin=v‖v‖=12[−110].

solution.reasoning: Q(x)=-(x_1-x_2)^2+2x_3^2≥-2(x_1^2+x_2^2)+2x_3^2=-2+4x_3^2≥-2. Equality holds when x_3=0 and x_1=-x_2. Option b has unit norm and satisfies these conditions, so Q(x)=-2. No captured Math Academy answer-key evidence is supplied.

\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 1

The minimum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=−x12−x22+2x32+2x1x2, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to −2. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
[110]
b
12[−110]
c
[001]
d
12[110]
e
[100]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[−1101−10002]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=−2:

A−(−2)I=[−1101−10002]−(−2)[100010001]=[110110004]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[−110].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umin=v‖v‖=12[−110].

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
question.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 2
?

The minimum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=7x12+8x22+5x32−4x2x3, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to 4. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
13[111]
b
12[122]
c
12[01−1]
d
15[012]
e
12[011]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[70008−20−25]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=4:

A−4I=[70008−20−25]−4[100010001]=[30004−20−21]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[012].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=5, we get

umin=v‖v‖=15[012].

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 2
?

The minimum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=7x12+8x22+5x32−4x2x3, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to 4. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
13[111]
b
12[122]
c
12[01−1]
d
15[012]
e
12[011]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[70008−20−25]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=4:

A−4I=[70008−20−25]−4[100010001]=[30004−20−21]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[012].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=5, we get

umin=v‖v‖=15[012].

solution.reasoning: For unit vectors, Q(x)=4+3x_1^2+(2x_2-x_3)^2≥4. The minimum is attained when x_1=0 and x_3=2x_2. Option d satisfies these conditions and has squared norm (1+4)/5=1. The mathematical answer is certain, but no captured Math Academy answer-key evidence is supplied.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 2
