The minimum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=7x12+8x22+5x32−4x2x3, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to 4. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
13[111]
b
12[122]
c
12[01−1]
d
15[012]
e
12[011]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[70008−20−25]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=4:

A−4I=[70008−20−25]−4[100010001]=[30004−20−21]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[012].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=5, we get

umin=v‖v‖=15[012].

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: The maximum  value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum  is attained?
question.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 3
?

The maximum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+x22+x32−6x1x2, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to 4. Which of the following is a vector x at which the maximum is attained?

a
12[101]
b
12[110]
c
12[−110]
d
12[−101]
e
12[011]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1−30−310001]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=4:

A−4I=[1−30−310001]−4[100010001]=[−3−30−3−3000−3]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[−110].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umax=v‖v‖=12[−110].

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$

$$

$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 3
?

The maximum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+x22+x32−6x1x2, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to 4. Which of the following is a vector x at which the maximum is attained?

a
12[101]
b
12[110]
c
12[−110]
d
12[−101]
e
12[011]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1−30−310001]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=4:

A−4I=[1−30−310001]−4[100010001]=[−3−30−3−3000−3]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[−110].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umax=v‖v‖=12[−110].

solution.reasoning: For unit vectors, 4-Q(x)=3(x_1+x_2)^2+3x_3^2≥0. Thus Q(x)≤4, with equality when x_1=-x_2 and x_3=0. Option c satisfies these conditions and has unit norm. No captured Math Academy answer-key evidence is supplied.

Question 3
?

The maximum value of the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+x22+x32−6x1x2, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to 4. Which of the following is a vector x at which the maximum is attained?

a
12[101]
b
12[110]
c
12[−110]
d
12[−101]
e
12[011]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let A be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

  • The maximum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of A: max{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmax The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umax.

  • The minimum value of Q(x), when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of A: min{Q(x)|‖x‖=1}=λmin The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector umin.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1−30−310001]

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=4:

A−4I=[1−30−310001]−4[100010001]=[−3−30−3−3000−3]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[−110].

Finally, dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umax=v‖v‖=12[−110].

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?
question.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 4
?

The maximum value of Q(x)=x12+16x1x2+4x22, when x12+4x22=4, is 20. Which of the following is a vector x at which the maximum is attained?

a
110[13]
b
15[−21]
c
110[−31]
d
12[1−1]
e
12[21]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1884]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

x1222+x2212=1

This is an ellipse with semiaxes a=2 (along the x1-axis) and b=1 (along the x2-axis). If we introduce new variables

y1=x12 and y2=x2,

the equation of the ellipse will transform into y12+y22=1 or ‖y‖=1.

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

P=[2001],

we obtain that x=Py. Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

Q(x)=xTAx=(Py)TA(Py)=yT(PTAP)y=Q′(y).

As a result, since PT=P, the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

B=PTAP=PAP=[2001][1884][2001]=[21684][2001]=[416164].

Now, we maximize Q′(y) when ‖y‖=1, as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is 20, we have

max{Q′(y)|‖y‖=1}=λmax=20.

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmax=20:

B−20I=[416164]−20[1001]=[−161616−16] Seeking a non-zero solution of (B−20I)y=0 gives the eigenvector v=[11]. Dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umax=v‖v‖=12[11].

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

xmax=Pumax=[2001]⋅12[11]=12[21]

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

The maximum value of Q(x)=x12+16x1x2+4x22, when x12+4x22=4, is 20. Which of the following is a vector x at which the maximum is attained?

a
110[13]
b
15[−21]
c
110[−31]
d
12[1−1]
e
12[21]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1884]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

x1222+x2212=1

This is an ellipse with semiaxes a=2 (along the x1-axis) and b=1 (along the x2-axis). If we introduce new variables

y1=x12 and y2=x2,

the equation of the ellipse will transform into y12+y22=1 or ‖y‖=1.

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

P=[2001],

we obtain that x=Py. Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

Q(x)=xTAx=(Py)TA(Py)=yT(PTAP)y=Q′(y).

As a result, since PT=P, the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

B=PTAP=PAP=[2001][1884][2001]=[21684][2001]=[416164].

Now, we maximize Q′(y) when ‖y‖=1, as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is 20, we have

max{Q′(y)|‖y‖=1}=λmax=20.

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmax=20:

B−20I=[416164]−20[1001]=[−161616−16] Seeking a non-zero solution of (B−20I)y=0 gives the eigenvector v=[11]. Dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umax=v‖v‖=12[11].

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

xmax=Pumax=[2001]⋅12[11]=12[21]

solution.reasoning: Under the constraint, Q(x)=4+16x_1x_2 and (x_1-2x_2)^2=4-4x_1x_2≥0, so x_1x_2≤1 and Q(x)≤20. Equality requires x_1=2x_2. Option e satisfies the constraint: x_1^2+4x_2^2=2+2=4, and its product x_1x_2=1 gives Q(x)=20. No captured Math Academy answer-key evidence is supplied.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4

The maximum value of Q(x)=x12+16x1x2+4x22, when x12+4x22=4, is 20. Which of the following is a vector x at which the maximum is attained?

a
110[13]
b
15[−21]
c
110[−31]
d
12[1−1]
e
12[21]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1884]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

x1222+x2212=1

This is an ellipse with semiaxes a=2 (along the x1-axis) and b=1 (along the x2-axis). If we introduce new variables

y1=x12 and y2=x2,

the equation of the ellipse will transform into y12+y22=1 or ‖y‖=1.

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

P=[2001],

we obtain that x=Py. Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

Q(x)=xTAx=(Py)TA(Py)=yT(PTAP)y=Q′(y).

As a result, since PT=P, the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

B=PTAP=PAP=[2001][1884][2001]=[21684][2001]=[416164].

Now, we maximize Q′(y) when ‖y‖=1, as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is 20, we have

max{Q′(y)|‖y‖=1}=λmax=20.

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmax=20:

B−20I=[416164]−20[1001]=[−161616−16] Seeking a non-zero solution of (B−20I)y=0 gives the eigenvector v=[11]. Dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umax=v‖v‖=12[11].

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

xmax=Pumax=[2001]⋅12[11]=12[21]

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: The minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
question.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}]+72[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

The minimum value of Q(x)=4x12−36x1x2+9x22, when 4x12+9x22=36, is −72. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
15[−23]
b
15[−12]
c
12[32]
d
110[21]
e
15[12]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[4−18−189]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

x1232+x2222=1

This is an ellipse with semiaxes a=3 (along the x1-axis) and b=2 (along the x2-axis). If we introduce new variables

y1=x13 and y2=x22,

the equation of the ellipse will transform into y12+y22=1 or ‖y‖=1.

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

P=[3002],

we obtain that x=Py. Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

Q(x)=xTAx=(Py)TA(Py)=yT(PTAP)y=Q′(y).

As a result, since PT=P, the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

B=PTAP=PAP=[3002][4−18−189][3002]=[12−54−3618][3002]=[36−108−10836].

Now, we minimize Q′(y) when ‖y‖=1, as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is −72, we have

min{Q′(y)|‖y‖=1}=λmin=−72.

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=−72:

B−(−72)I=[36−108−10836]+72[1001]=[108−108−108108] Seeking a non-zero solution of (B−(−72)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[11]. Dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umin=v‖v‖=12[11].

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

xmin=Pumin=[3002]⋅12[11]=12[32]

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}]+72[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

The minimum value of Q(x)=4x12−36x1x2+9x22, when 4x12+9x22=36, is −72. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
15[−23]
b
15[−12]
c
12[32]
d
110[21]
e
15[12]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[4−18−189]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

x1232+x2222=1

This is an ellipse with semiaxes a=3 (along the x1-axis) and b=2 (along the x2-axis). If we introduce new variables

y1=x13 and y2=x22,

the equation of the ellipse will transform into y12+y22=1 or ‖y‖=1.

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

P=[3002],

we obtain that x=Py. Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

Q(x)=xTAx=(Py)TA(Py)=yT(PTAP)y=Q′(y).

As a result, since PT=P, the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

B=PTAP=PAP=[3002][4−18−189][3002]=[12−54−3618][3002]=[36−108−10836].

Now, we minimize Q′(y) when ‖y‖=1, as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is −72, we have

min{Q′(y)|‖y‖=1}=λmin=−72.

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=−72:

B−(−72)I=[36−108−10836]+72[1001]=[108−108−108108] Seeking a non-zero solution of (B−(−72)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[11]. Dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umin=v‖v‖=12[11].

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

xmin=Pumin=[3002]⋅12[11]=12[32]

solution.reasoning: Under the constraint, Q(x)+72=3(2x_1-3x_2)^2≥0. Thus the minimum is -72, attained when 2x_1=3x_2. Option c satisfies this equality and the constraint: 4(9/2)+9(4/2)=36. No captured Math Academy answer-key evidence is supplied.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: The minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}]+72[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

The minimum value of Q(x)=4x12−36x1x2+9x22, when 4x12+9x22=36, is −72. Which of the following is a vector x at which the minimum is attained?

a
15[−23]
b
15[−12]
c
12[32]
d
110[21]
e
15[12]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[4−18−189]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

x1232+x2222=1

This is an ellipse with semiaxes a=3 (along the x1-axis) and b=2 (along the x2-axis). If we introduce new variables

y1=x13 and y2=x22,

the equation of the ellipse will transform into y12+y22=1 or ‖y‖=1.

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

P=[3002],

we obtain that x=Py. Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

Q(x)=xTAx=(Py)TA(Py)=yT(PTAP)y=Q′(y).

As a result, since PT=P, the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

B=PTAP=PAP=[3002][4−18−189][3002]=[12−54−3618][3002]=[36−108−10836].

Now, we minimize Q′(y) when ‖y‖=1, as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is −72, we have

min{Q′(y)|‖y‖=1}=λmin=−72.

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmin=−72:

B−(−72)I=[36−108−10836]+72[1001]=[108−108−108108] Seeking a non-zero solution of (B−(−72)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v=[11]. Dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=2, we get

umin=v‖v‖=12[11].

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

xmin=Pumin=[3002]⋅12[11]=12[32]

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14198813/assets/7defdf7c31a164fdbe702c1f5e87567f5da868d7530143493f9713ff88de98bc.png)

Find ${lim}_{x\to \,-\frac{3}{2}}f(x)$ for the function above.
questions.worked_solution:
As $x$ approaches $-\frac{3}{2},$ the value of $f(x)$ approaches $2.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-\frac{3}{2}}f(x)=2\,.
$$

Remember, it does not matter that the actual value of $f(-\frac{3}{2})$ is $0.$ All that matters is that as $x$ approaches $-\frac{3}{2},$ the function $f(x)$ *looks like* it is getting closer and closer to $2.$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14198813/assets/f8b33f31c4b569da24aa8235421698859e74b144e783f0fb917a5f4b3679d834.png)

Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above?

I. ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=3$

II. ${lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=1$

III. ${lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. As $x$ approaches $0,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=2.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=2.
$$

- Statement II is true. As $x$ approaches $-1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=1.
$$

- Statement III is false. As $x$ approaches $-2,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=0,$ and consequently 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)=0.
$$

 
Similarly, as $x$ approaches $1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1,$ and consequently,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=1.
$$

As a result,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x).
$$

In conclusion, only statement II is true.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying True Statements About Limits
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown below? 

I. $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0}f(x)=0$

II. $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,3}f(x)=0$

III. $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)=\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x)$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14198813/assets/68241f3cd913cd91d10765499dc4ce4398fb3e8a81ec4bcfb65b47c0d77731d6.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. As $x$ approaches $0,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=-1.$ Consequently, 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0}f(x)=-1.
$$

- Statement II is true. As $x$ approaches $3,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=0.$ Consequently,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,3}f(x)=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. As $x$ approaches $-1$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=2,$ and consequently

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)=2.
$$

Similiarly, as $x$ approaches $1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=-2,$ and consequently

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x)=-2.
$$

As a result,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)\ne\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x).
$$

In conclusion, only statement II is true.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **limit** of a function is the value that the function approaches. For example, the function $y=f(x)$ shown below is not defined at $x=2,$ as represented by the open circle there $-$ but when we *approach* $x=2$, we see that $f(x)$ *approaches* the value $y=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14198813/assets/f7081d649c6cdfa0a19a0fb2de93b97ee700ad922f34530c7f3e5c2a3228c9fb.png)

As $x$ approaches $2$, the value of $f(x)$ approaches $1.$ In other words, the limit of $f(x),$ as $x$ approaches $2,$ is $1$. We can express this mathematically as 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}f(x)=1 \, .
$$

tutorials.name: Limit Has Nothing to Do With the Function Value
tutorials.problem:
The limit of a function at some point has **nothing to do** with the value of the function at that point.

For example, the following functions $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ have *different values* at $x=2,$ but they have the *same limit* at $x=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14198813/assets/6a73b74072a8a990c91a38553d519f4913370d34ef0251b7e45cc664da40517d.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14198813/assets/06e150aacae774b4fe883a2750ef13cebbddf2ea871e5a682f2587c47a54615a.png)

The actual values of $g(2)$ and $h(2)$ are irrelevant for determining the limit at $x=2$. All that matters is what values the functions *look like* they are approaching as $x$ approaches $2$. 

Near $x=2,$ both $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ appear to be approaching $y=1$. Therefore,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}g(x)=1
$$

and

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}h(x)=1 \, .
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14198813/assets/c0ed78e2e640611d70263e17a76eb4a13e9e2816efba02494b53e540d38065d6.png)
question.worked_solution:
As $x$ approaches $0,$ the value of $f(x)$ approaches $1.$ Consequently, 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0}f(x)= 1\,.
$$

Remember, it does not matter that the actual value of $f(0)$ is $2.$ All that matters is that as $x$ approaches $0,$ the function $f(x)$ *looks like* it is getting closer and closer to $1$.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Limit When the Limit is Not Equal to the Function Value
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. As $x$ approaches $0,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=-1.$ Consequently, 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,0}f(x)=-1.
$$

- Statement II is true. As $x$ approaches $3,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=0.$ Consequently,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,3}f(x)=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. As $x$ approaches $-1$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=2,$ and consequently

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)=2.
$$

Similiarly, as $x$ approaches $1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=-2,$ and consequently

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x)=-2.
$$

As a result,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)\ne\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x).
$$

In conclusion, only statement II is true.

$$

- Statement III is false. As $x$ approaches $-1$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=2,$ and consequently

Similiarly, as $x$ approaches $1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=-2,$ and consequently

As a result,

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,-1}f(x)\ne\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \,1}f(x).

In conclusion, only statement II is true.

Find ${lim}_{x\to \,-\frac{3}{2}}f(x)$ for the function above.
question.worked_solution:
As $x$ approaches $-\frac{3}{2},$ the value of $f(x)$ approaches $2.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-\frac{3}{2}}f(x)=2\,.
$$

Remember, it does not matter that the actual value of $f(-\frac{3}{2})$ is $0.$ All that matters is that as $x$ approaches $-\frac{3}{2},$ the function $f(x)$ *looks like* it is getting closer and closer to $2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14198813/assets/f8b33f31c4b569da24aa8235421698859e74b144e783f0fb917a5f4b3679d834.png)

Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above?

I. ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=3$

II. ${lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=1$

III. ${lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)$
question.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. As $x$ approaches $0,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=2.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=2.
$$

- Statement II is true. As $x$ approaches $-1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=1.
$$

- Statement III is false. As $x$ approaches $-2,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=0,$ and consequently 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)=0.
$$

 
Similarly, as $x$ approaches $1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1,$ and consequently,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=1.
$$

As a result,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x).
$$

In conclusion, only statement II is true.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14198813/assets/f8b33f31c4b569da24aa8235421698859e74b144e783f0fb917a5f4b3679d834.png)

Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above?

I. ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=3$

II. ${lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=1$

III. ${lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. As $x$ approaches $0,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=2.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=2.
$$

- Statement II is true. As $x$ approaches $-1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=1.
$$

- Statement III is false. As $x$ approaches $-2,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=0,$ and consequently 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)=0.
$$

 
Similarly, as $x$ approaches $1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1,$ and consequently,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=1.
$$

As a result,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x).
$$

In conclusion, only statement II is true.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
The table shows probabilities in the form $P(X\ge x).$ So first, we express the desired probability in this form:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge x) & =1-P(X\le x) \\  & =1-0.9 \\  & =0.1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $X∼{T}_{19},$ we focus on the row of the table that corresponds to $k=19.$

| $k∖p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $19$ | $1.328$ | $1.729$ | $2.093$ | $2.539$ | $2.861$ |
| $20$ | $1.325$ | $1.725$ | $2.086$ | $2.528$ | $2.845$ |
| $21$ | $1.323$ | $1.721$ | $2.080$ | $2.518$ | $2.831$ |

From this row, we see that

$$
P(X\ge 1.328)=0.100.
$$

Therefore, our answer is $x=1.328.$

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005

questions.name: Question 3
questions.worked_solution:
The table shows probabilities in the form $P(X\ge x).$ So first, we express the desired probability in this form:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge x) & =1-P(X\le x) \\  & =1-0.995 \\  & =0.005\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $X∼{T}_{25},$ we focus on the row of the table that corresponds to $k=25.$

| $k∖p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $24$ | $1.318$ | $1.711$ | $2.064$ | $2.492$ | $2.797$ |
| $25$ | $1.316$ | $1.708$ | $2.060$ | $2.485$ | $2.787$ |
| $26$ | $1.315$ | $1.706$ | $2.056$ | $2.479$ | $2.779$ |

From this row, we see that

$$
P(X\ge 2.787)=0.005.
$$

Therefore, our answer is $x=2.787.$

Question 4
?

The table below gives the values of x that satisfy P(X≥x)=p, where X has a student's t-distribution Tk with k degrees of freedom. Given that the random variable X∼T15, find the value of x such that P(|X|≥x)=0.02.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
15 1.341 1.753 2.131 2.602 2.947
16 1.337 1.746 2.120 2.583 2.921
17 1.333 1.740 2.110 2.576 2.898
a
1.337
b
1.341
c
2.567
d
2.602
e
2.131
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Due to the symmetry of the student's t-distribution, we have that P(|X|≥x)=0.02 is equivalent to

2P(X≥x)=0.02⟹P(X≥x)=0.01.

Now, since X∼T15, we focus on the row of the table that corresponds to k=15.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
15 1.341 1.753 2.131 2.602 2.947
16 1.337 1.746 2.120 2.583 2.921
17 1.333 1.740 2.110 2.567 2.898

From this row, we see that P(X≥2.602)=0.010.

Therefore, our answer is x=2.602.

question.html:
Question 1
?

The table below gives the values of x that satisfy P(X≥x)=p, where X has a student's t-distribution Tk with k degrees of freedom. Given that the random variable X∼T19, find the value of x such that P(X≤x)=0.9.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
19 1.328 1.729 2.093 2.539 2.861
20 1.325 1.725 2.086 2.528 2.845
21 1.323 1.721 2.080 2.518 2.831
a
1.328
b
2.528
c
2.539
d
2.861
e
1.323
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The table shows probabilities in the form P(X≥x). So first, we express the desired probability in this form:

P(X≥x)=1−P(X≤x)=1−0.9=0.1

Now, since X∼T19, we focus on the row of the table that corresponds to k=19.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
19 1.328 1.729 2.093 2.539 2.861
20 1.325 1.725 2.086 2.528 2.845
21 1.323 1.721 2.080 2.518 2.831

From this row, we see that P(X≥1.328)=0.100.

Therefore, our answer is x=1.328.

solution.reasoning: The t-distribution is continuous, so P(X≤x)=0.9 implies P(X≥x)=0.1. In the k=19 row and p=0.100 column, x=1.328, which is option a. The mathematics is conclusive, but no Math Academy answer-key evidence was captured.

question.html:
Question 2
?

The table below gives the values of x that satisfy P(X≥x)=p, where X has a student's t-distribution Tk with k degrees of freedom. Given that the random variable X∼T20, find the value of x such that P(X≤x)=0.99.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
19 1.328 1.729 2.093 2.539 2.861
20 1.325 1.725 2.086 2.528 2.845
21 1.323 1.721 2.080 2.518 2.831
a
 2.518
b
 1.325
c
 2.528
d
 1.328
e
 2.845
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The table shows probabilities in the form P(X≥x). So first, we express the desired probability in this form:

P(X≥x)=1−P(X≤x)=1−0.99=0.01

Now, since X∼T20, we focus on the row of the table that corresponds to k=20.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
19 1.328 1.729 2.093 2.539 2.861
20 1.325 1.725 2.086 2.528 2.845
21 1.323 1.721 2.080 2.518 2.831

From this row, we see that P(X≥2.528)=0.010.

Therefore, our answer is x=2.528.

solution.reasoning: Continuity gives P(X≥x)=1−0.99=0.010. The k=20 row and p=0.010 column give x=2.528, option c. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was captured.

question.html:
Question 3
?

The table below gives the values of x that satisfy P(X≥x)=p, where X has a student's t-distribution Tk with k degrees of freedom. Given that the random variable X∼T25, find the value of x such that P(X≤x)=0.995.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
24 1.318 1.711 2.064 2.492 2.797
25 1.316 1.708 2.060 2.485 2.787
26 1.315 1.706 2.056 2.479 2.779
a
2.787
b
2.779
c
1.708
d
2.485
e
1.318
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The table shows probabilities in the form P(X≥x). So first, we express the desired probability in this form:

P(X≥x)=1−P(X≤x)=1−0.995=0.005

Now, since X∼T25, we focus on the row of the table that corresponds to k=25.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
24 1.318 1.711 2.064 2.492 2.797
25 1.316 1.708 2.060 2.485 2.787
26 1.315 1.706 2.056 2.479 2.779

From this row, we see that P(X≥2.787)=0.005.

Therefore, our answer is x=2.787.

solution.reasoning: Since the t-distribution is continuous, P(X≥x)=1−0.995=0.005. The k=25 row and p=0.005 column give x=2.787, option a. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was captured.

$$

$$

Now, since $X∼{T}_{25},$ we focus on the row of the table that corresponds to $k=25.$

| $k∖p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $24$ | $1.318$ | $1.711$ | $2.064$ | $2.492$ | $2.797$ |
| $25$ | $1.316$ | $1.708$ | $2.060$ | $2.485$ | $2.787$ |
| $26$ | $1.315$ | $1.706$ | $2.056$ | $2.479$ | $2.779$ |

From this row, we see that

$$
P(X\ge 2.787)=0.005.
$$

Therefore, our answer is $x=2.787.$

Question 4
?

The table below gives the values of x that satisfy P(X≥x)=p, where X has a student's t-distribution Tk with k degrees of freedom. Given that the random variable X∼T15, find the value of x such that P(|X|≥x)=0.02.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
15 1.341 1.753 2.131 2.602 2.947
16 1.337 1.746 2.120 2.583 2.921
17 1.333 1.740 2.110 2.576 2.898
a
1.337
b
1.341
c
2.567
d
2.602
e
2.131
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Due to the symmetry of the student's t-distribution, we have that P(|X|≥x)=0.02 is equivalent to

2P(X≥x)=0.02⟹P(X≥x)=0.01.

Now, since X∼T15, we focus on the row of the table that corresponds to k=15.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
15 1.341 1.753 2.131 2.602 2.947
16 1.337 1.746 2.120 2.583 2.921
17 1.333 1.740 2.110 2.567 2.898

From this row, we see that P(X≥2.602)=0.010.

Therefore, our answer is x=2.602.

solution.reasoning: By symmetry of the t-distribution, P(|X|≥x)=2P(X≥x) for x>0. Thus each tail has probability 0.02/2=0.010. The k=15 row and p=0.010 column give x=2.602, option d. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was captured.

question.html:
Question 5
?

The table below gives the values of x that satisfy P(X≥x)=p, where X has a student's t-distribution Tk with k degrees of freedom. Given that the random variable X∼T25, find the value of x such that P(|X|≥x)=0.01.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
24 1.318 1.711 2.064 2.492 2.797
25 1.316 1.708 2.060 2.485 2.787
26 1.315 1.706 2.056 2.479 2.779
a
1.708
b
2.787
c
2.479
d
2.485
e
2.797
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Due to the symmetry of the student's t-distribution, we have that P(|X|≥x)=0.01 is equivalent to

2P(X≥x)=0.01⟹P(X≥x)=0.005.

Now, since X∼T25, we focus on the row of the table that corresponds to k=25.

k∖p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
24 1.318 1.711 2.064 2.492 2.797
25 1.316 1.708 2.060 2.485 2.787
26 1.315 1.706 2.056 2.479 2.779

From this row, we see that P(X≥2.787)=0.005.

Therefore, our answer is x=2.787.

solution.reasoning: By symmetry, P(|X|≥x)=2P(X≥x) for x>0, so each tail has probability 0.01/2=0.005. The k=25 row and p=0.005 column give x=2.787, option b. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was captured.

feedback.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198128/assets/635de7075b0d106ffc2a0f15e65ca7a3406a49945591aa5eae59090c74df1398.png)

Due to the symmetry of the student's $t$-distribution, we have that $P(|X|\ge x)=0.01$ is equivalent to

$$
2P(X\ge x)=0.01\,⟹\,P(X\ge x)=0.005.
$$

Now, since $X∼{T}_{25},$ we focus on the row of the table that corresponds to $k=25.$

| $k∖p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $24$ | $1.318$ | $1.711$ | $2.064$ | $2.492$ | $2.797$ |
| $25$ | $1.316$ | $1.708$ | $2.060$ | $2.485$ | $2.787$ |
| $26$ | $1.315$ | $1.706$ | $2.056$ | $2.479$ | $2.779$ |

From this row, we see that

$$
P(X\ge 2.787)=0.005.
$$

Therefore, our answer is $x=2.787.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$

$\operatorname{csch}⁡(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=$
questions.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csch}⁡(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{2}^{-2}}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{2}^{-2}-{2}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{1}{4}-4)} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-\frac{15}{4})} \\  & =-\frac{8}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
$$
Evaluate $\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}).$ **Do not round** your answer.

$$
$\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5})=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}-{e}^{-(-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5})}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{(\sqrt{5})}^{-1}}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}-\sqrt{5})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{1-5}{\sqrt{5}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}})} \\  & =2\times (-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
$$

$\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\sqrt{3})=$
questions.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\sqrt{3}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\sqrt{3}}-{e}^{-(-\sqrt{3})}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\sqrt{3}}-{e}^{\sqrt{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
$$

Given that $t>0,$ which of the following is equivalent to $\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t})?$
questions.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{t})^{-1}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}+(\sqrt{t})^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\sqrt{t}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{t}})} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{t}}{t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
Evaluate $\operatorname{sech}⁡1.$ **Do not round** your answer.

$$
$\operatorname{sech}⁡1=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡1 & =\frac{2}{{e}^{1}+{e}^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(e+\frac{1}{e})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{{e}^{2}+1}{e})} \\  & =\frac{2e}{{e}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
$$

Given that $z>0,$ which of the following is equivalent to $\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡z) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡z}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{z}^{-1}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{z+(z)^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(z+\frac{1}{z})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{{z}^{2}+1}{z})} \\  & =\frac{2z}{{z}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
$$
Evaluate $\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}).$ **Do not round** your answer.

$$
$\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5})=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{5})^{-1}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}+(\sqrt{5})^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\sqrt{5}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{6}{\sqrt{5}})} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csch}⁡(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{2}^{-2}}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{2}^{-2}-{2}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{1}{4}-4)} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-\frac{15}{4})} \\  & =-\frac{8}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csch}⁡(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{2}^{-2}}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{2}^{-2}-{2}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{1}{4}-4)} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-\frac{15}{4})} \\  & =-\frac{8}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

?

a
2e7t−e−7t
b
2e7t+e−7t
c
2e7t+e−7t
d
2e7t−e−7t
e
2e−7t−e7t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definition of csch⁡x is

csch⁡x=1sinh⁡x=2ex−e−x.

Therefore, csch⁡(7t)=2e7t−e−7t.

Question 5
?

csch⁡(−5)=

a
2e−5−e5
b
2e−5+e5
c
2e5−e−5
d
2e−1/5−e1/5
e
2e−1/5+e1/5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of csch⁡x is

csch⁡x=1sinh⁡x=2ex−e−x.

Therefore, csch⁡(−5)=2e−5−e−(−5)=2e−5−e5.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{t})^{-1}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}+(\sqrt{t})^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\sqrt{t}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{t}})} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{t}}{t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
$$

Given that $t>0,$ which of the following is equivalent to $\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t})?$
question.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{t})^{-1}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}+(\sqrt{t})^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\sqrt{t}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{t}})} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{t}}{t+1}.\end{aligned}

Question 6
?

Given that t>0, which of the following is equivalent to sech⁡(ln⁡t)?

a
tt+1
b
tt+1
c
2tt+1
d
2tt+1
e
5tt+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of sech⁡x is sech⁡x=1cosh⁡x=2ex+e−x.

Therefore,

sech⁡(ln⁡t)=2eln⁡t+e−ln⁡t=2eln⁡t+eln⁡(t)−1=2t+(t)−1=2(t+1t)=2(t+1t)=2tt+1.

$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{5})^{-1}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}+(\sqrt{5})^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\sqrt{5}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{6}{\sqrt{5}})} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\operatorname{coth}⁡x & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{tanh}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}+1}{{e}^{2x}-1} \\  & =\frac{1+{e}^{-2x}}{1-{e}^{-2x}}.\end{aligned}

$$

$\operatorname{csch}⁡(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=$
question.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csch}⁡(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-(-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{2}^{-2}}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{2}^{-2}-{2}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{1}{4}-4)} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-\frac{15}{4})} \\  & =-\frac{8}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

csch⁡(−2ln⁡2)=

a

 815

EXPLANATION

The definition of csch⁡x is

csch⁡x=1sinh⁡x=2ex−e−x.

Therefore, csch⁡(−2ln⁡2)=2e−2ln⁡2−e−(−2ln⁡2)=2e−2ln⁡2−e2ln⁡2=2eln⁡2−2−eln⁡22=22−2−22=2(14−4)=2(−154)=−815.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
Evaluate $\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}).$ **Do not round** your answer.

$$
$\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5})=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}-{e}^{-(-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5})}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{(\sqrt{5})}^{-1}}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{5}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}-\sqrt{5})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{1-5}{\sqrt{5}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}})} \\  & =2\times (-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that t≠0, which of the following is equivalent to csch⁡(7t)?

a
2e7t−e−7t
b
2e7t+e−7t
c
2e7t+e−7t
d
2e7t−e−7t
e
2e−7t−e7t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definition of csch⁡x is

csch⁡x=1sinh⁡x=2ex−e−x.

Therefore, csch⁡(7t)=2e7t−e−7t.

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that t≠0, which of the following is equivalent to csch⁡(7t)?

a
2e7t−e−7t
b
2e7t+e−7t
c
2e7t+e−7t
d
2e7t−e−7t
e
2e−7t−e7t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definition of csch⁡x is

csch⁡x=1sinh⁡x=2ex−e−x.

Therefore, csch⁡(7t)=2e7t−e−7t.
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating Hyperbolic Cosecant

solution.reasoning: By definition, \operatorname{csch}x=2/(e^x-e^{-x}). Substituting x=\sqrt{7}\,t gives option a. For real t\ne0, its denominator is nonzero. The supplied example supports this identity, but no Math Academy answer key or grade for the current question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
$$

Given that $t\ne 0,$ which of the following is equivalent to $\operatorname{csch}⁡(\sqrt{7}\,t)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡(\sqrt{7}\,t)=\frac{2}{{e}^{\sqrt{7}\,t}-{e}^{-\sqrt{7}\,t}}.
$$

Question 3

Given that t≠0, which of the following is equivalent to csch⁡(7t)?

a
2e7t−e−7t
b
2e7t+e−7t
c
2e7t+e−7t
d
2e7t−e−7t
e
2e−7t−e7t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definition of csch⁡x is

csch⁡x=1sinh⁡x=2ex−e−x.

Therefore, csch⁡(7t)=2e7t−e−7t.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$

$\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\sqrt{3})=$
question.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\sqrt{3}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\sqrt{3}}-{e}^{-(-\sqrt{3})}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\sqrt{3}}-{e}^{\sqrt{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore,

\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\sqrt{3}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\sqrt{3}}-{e}^{-(-\sqrt{3})}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\sqrt{3}}-{e}^{\sqrt{3}}}.\end{aligned}

solution.reasoning: Using \operatorname{csch}x=2/(e^x-e^{-x}) with x=-\sqrt{3} gives 2/(e^{-\sqrt{3}}-e^{\sqrt{3}}), which is option c. The supplied example supports the formula, but no Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
$$

$\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\sqrt{3})=$
feedback.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csch}⁡(-\sqrt{3}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\sqrt{3}}-{e}^{-(-\sqrt{3})}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{-\sqrt{3}}-{e}^{\sqrt{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

csch⁡(−5)=

a
2e−5−e5
b
2e−5+e5
c
2e5−e−5
d
2e−1/5−e1/5
e
2e−1/5+e1/5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of csch⁡x is

csch⁡x=1sinh⁡x=2ex−e−x.

Therefore, csch⁡(−5)=2e−5−e−(−5)=2e−5−e5.

Question 5
?

csch⁡(−5)=

a
2e−5−e5
b
2e−5+e5
c
2e5−e−5
d
2e−1/5−e1/5
e
2e−1/5+e1/5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of csch⁡x is

csch⁡x=1sinh⁡x=2ex−e−x.

Therefore, csch⁡(−5)=2e−5−e−(−5)=2e−5−e5.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
$$

Given that $t>0,$ which of the following is equivalent to $\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t})?$
question.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{t})^{-1}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}+(\sqrt{t})^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\sqrt{t}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{t}})} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{t}}{t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Given that t>0, which of the following is equivalent to sech⁡(ln⁡t)?

a
tt+1
b
tt+1
c
2tt+1
d
2tt+1
e
5tt+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of sech⁡x is sech⁡x=1cosh⁡x=2ex+e−x.

Therefore,

sech⁡(ln⁡t)=2eln⁡t+e−ln⁡t=2eln⁡t+eln⁡(t)−1=2t+(t)−1=2(t+1t)=2(t+1t)=2tt+1.

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.\end{aligned}

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{t})^{-1}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}+(\sqrt{t})^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\sqrt{t}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{t}})} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{t}}{t+1}.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 6
?

Given that t>0, which of the following is equivalent to sech⁡(ln⁡t)?

a
tt+1
b
tt+1
c
2tt+1
d
2tt+1
e
5tt+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of sech⁡x is sech⁡x=1cosh⁡x=2ex+e−x.

Therefore,

sech⁡(ln⁡t)=2eln⁡t+e−ln⁡t=2eln⁡t+eln⁡(t)−1=2t+(t)−1=2(t+1t)=2(t+1t)=2tt+1.
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating Hyperbolic Secant

solution.reasoning: Using \operatorname{sech}x=2/(e^x+e^{-x}), we obtain 2/(\sqrt{t}+1/\sqrt{t})=2\sqrt{t}/(t+1), which is option d. This is valid for t>0. The supplied example supports the formula, but no Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

Question 6
?

Given that t>0, which of the following is equivalent to sech⁡(ln⁡t)?

a
tt+1
b
tt+1
c
2tt+1
d
2tt+1
e
5tt+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of sech⁡x is sech⁡x=1cosh⁡x=2ex+e−x.

Therefore,

sech⁡(ln⁡t)=2eln⁡t+e−ln⁡t=2eln⁡t+eln⁡(t)−1=2t+(t)−1=2(t+1t)=2(t+1t)=2tt+1.

question.problem:
$$
Evaluate $\operatorname{sech}⁡1.$ **Do not round** your answer.

$$
$\operatorname{sech}⁡1=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡1 & =\frac{2}{{e}^{1}+{e}^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(e+\frac{1}{e})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{{e}^{2}+1}{e})} \\  & =\frac{2e}{{e}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
$$

Given that $z>0,$ which of the following is equivalent to $\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡z)?$
question.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡z) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡z}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{z}^{-1}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{z+(z)^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(z+\frac{1}{z})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{{z}^{2}+1}{z})} \\  & =\frac{2z}{{z}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Given that z>0, which of the following is equivalent to sech⁡(ln⁡z)?

a
2z1−z2
b
2zz2−1
c
zz2+1
d
2zz2+1
e
zz2−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of sech⁡x is sech⁡x=1cosh⁡x=2ex+e−x.

Therefore,

sech⁡(ln⁡z)=2eln⁡z+e−ln⁡z=2eln⁡z+eln⁡z−1=2z+(z)−1=2(z+1z)=2(z2+1z)=2zz2+1.

question.html:
Question 8
?

Given that z>0, which of the following is equivalent to sech⁡(ln⁡z)?

a
2z1−z2
b
2zz2−1
c
zz2+1
d
2zz2+1
e
zz2−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of sech⁡x is sech⁡x=1cosh⁡x=2ex+e−x.

Therefore,

sech⁡(ln⁡z)=2eln⁡z+e−ln⁡z=2eln⁡z+eln⁡z−1=2z+(z)−1=2(z+1z)=2(z2+1z)=2zz2+1.
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating Hyperbolic Secant

solution.reasoning: Using \operatorname{sech}x=2/(e^x+e^{-x}) and z>0, we get \operatorname{sech}(\ln z)=2/(z+1/z)=2z/(z^2+1), which is option d. The supplied example supports the formula, but no Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.problem:
$$

Given that $z>0,$ which of the following is equivalent to $\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡z)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{sech}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}=\frac{2}{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡z) & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡z}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{z}^{-1}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{z+(z)^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(z+\frac{1}{z})} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\frac{{z}^{2}+1}{z})} \\  & =\frac{2z}{{z}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}

$$

$$

$$

The definition of $\operatorname{coth}⁡x$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{coth}⁡x & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{tanh}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}+1}{{e}^{2x}-1} \\  & =\frac{1+{e}^{-2x}}{1-{e}^{-2x}}.\end{aligned}

$$

EXPLANATION

The definition of coth⁡x is

coth⁡x=1tanh⁡x=ex+e−xex−e−x=e2x+1e2x−1=1+e−2x1−e−2x.

Using the third definition, we get

question.problem:
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to  $\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2w)?$
question.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{coth}⁡x$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{coth}⁡x & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{tanh}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}+1}{{e}^{2x}-1} \\  & =\frac{1+{e}^{-2x}}{1-{e}^{-2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the third definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2w) & =\frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2w}+1}{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2w}-1} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4{w}^{2}}+1}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4{w}^{2}}-1} \\  & =\frac{4{w}^{2}+1}{4{w}^{2}-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

Which of the following is equivalent to coth⁡(ln⁡2w)?

a
2w2−12w2+1
b
4w2−14w2+1
c
2w2+12w2−1
d
4w+14w−1
e
4w2+14w2−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of coth⁡x is coth⁡x=1tanh⁡x=ex+e−xex−e−x=e2x+1e2x−1=1+e−2x1−e−2x.

Using the third definition, we get coth⁡(ln⁡2w)=e2ln⁡2w+1e2ln⁡2w−1=eln⁡4w2+1eln⁡4w2−1=4w2+14w2−1.

question.html:
Question 14
?

Which of the following is equivalent to coth⁡(ln⁡2w)?

a
2w2−12w2+1
b
4w2−14w2+1
c
2w2+12w2−1
d
4w+14w−1
e
4w2+14w2−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of coth⁡x is coth⁡x=1tanh⁡x=ex+e−xex−e−x=e2x+1e2x−1=1+e−2x1−e−2x.

Using the third definition, we get coth⁡(ln⁡2w)=e2ln⁡2w+1e2ln⁡2w−1=eln⁡4w2+1eln⁡4w2−1=4w2+14w2−1.
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating Hyperbolic Cotangent

solution.reasoning: Using \operatorname{coth}x=(e^{2x}+1)/(e^{2x}-1) with x=\ln(2w), we have e^{2\ln(2w)}=(2w)^2=4w^2. Thus the equivalent expression is option e, on the original real domain w>0 and w\ne1/2. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

a
2w2−12w2+1
b
4w2−14w2+1
c
2w2+12w2−1
d
4w+14w−1
e
4w2+14w2−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definition of coth⁡x is coth⁡x=1tanh⁡x=ex+e−xex−e−x=e2x+1e2x−1=1+e−2x1−e−2x.

Using the third definition, we get coth⁡(ln⁡2w)=e2ln⁡2w+1e2ln⁡2w−1=eln⁡4w2+1eln⁡4w2−1=4w2+14w2−1.

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
$$
Evaluate $\operatorname{coth}⁡(\sqrt{5}).$ **Do not round** your answer.

$$
$\operatorname{coth}⁡(\sqrt{5})=$
 {{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
$$

The definition of $\operatorname{coth}⁡x$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{coth}⁡x & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{tanh}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}+1}{{e}^{2x}-1} \\  & =\frac{1+{e}^{-2x}}{1-{e}^{-2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the third definition, we get

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡(\sqrt{5})=\frac{{e}^{2\sqrt{5}}+1}{{e}^{2\sqrt{5}}-1}.
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(5,10)$ and $Y∼N(6,11).$ Find the distribution of the random variable $W=2X-5Y.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2})$, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}W=2X-5Y & ∼N(2\cdot 5+(-5)\cdot 6,{2}^{2}\cdot 10+(-5)^{2}\cdot 11) \\  & ∼N(-20,315).\end{aligned}
$$

 
Therefore, $W∼N(-20,315).$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),$ and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=4{X}_{1}-2{X}_{2} & ∼N(4{\mu }_{1}-2{\mu }_{2},16{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+4{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(20-16,48+16) \\  & ∼N(4,64).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =4$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{64}=8.$ 

We want to find $P(Y<14).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<14) & =P(Z<\frac{14-4}{8}) \\  & =P(Z<1.25) \\  & =Φ(1.25)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.25)≈0.8944.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(Y<14)≈0.89.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
The weights of some chocolate cookies are normally distributed with a mean of $10\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $1\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$ The weights of some oatcakes are normally distributed with a mean of $15\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $2\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$  If one chocolate cookie and one oatcake are randomly selected, what is the probability that $6$ times the weight of the cookie plus $4$ times the weight of oatcake is less than $120\,\text{g}$, but more than $100\,\text{g}?$ You may assume that the weights of the cookies and oatcakes are independent. 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-2.5\,$ | $\,0.0062\,$ | $\,0.0060\,$ | $\,0.0059\,$ | $\,0.0057\,$ | $\,0.0055\,$ |
| $\,-2.4\,$ | $\,0.0082\,$ | $\,0.0080\,$ | $\,0.0078\,$ | $\,0.0075\,$ | $\,0.0073\,$ |
| $\,-2.3\,$ | $\,0.0107\,$ | $\,0.0104\,$ | $\,0.0102\,$ | $\,0.0099\,$ | $\,0.0096\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let $X$ denote the weight of a chocolate cookie, and let $Y$ denote the weight of an oatcake. We want to find 

$$
P(100<6X+4Y<120).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X∼N(10,1)$ and $Y∼N(15,2),$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}6X+4Y & ∼N(6\cdot 10+4\cdot 15,36\cdot 1+16\cdot 2) \\  & ∼N(120,68).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $6X+4Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =120$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{68}.$

To find $P(100<6X+4Y<120),$ we convert $6X+4Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(100<6X+4Y<120) & =P(\frac{100-120}{\sqrt{68}}<Z<\frac{120-120}{\sqrt{68}}) \\  & ≈P(-2.43<Z<0) \\  & =P(Z<0)-P(Z\le -2.43) \\  & =P(Z\le 0)-P(Z\le -2.43) \\  & =Φ(0)-Φ(-2.43)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-2.43) & ≈0.0075,\end{aligned}
$$

and we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0) & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(100<6X+4Y<120) & ≈Φ(0)-Φ(-2.43) \\  & =0.5-0.0075 \\  & ≈0.4925.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
A factory produces shovels, each consisting of a handle and a blade.
The length of a handle is normally distributed with a mean of $120$ centimeters and a variance of $0.14,$  while the length of a blade is normally distributed with a mean of $30$ centimeters and a variance of $0.02.$ If one shovel is randomly selected, what is the probability that its length is more than $150$ centimeters, but less than $150.5$ centimeters? You may assume that the lengths are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8944\,$ | $\,0.8962\,$ | $\,0.8980\,$ | $\,0.8997\,$ | $\,0.9015\,$ |
| $\,1.3\,$ | $\,0.9115\,$ | $\,0.9131\,$ | $\,0.9147\,$ | $\,0.9162\,$ | $\,0.9177\,$ |
| $\,1.4\,$ | $\,0.9265\,$ | $\,0.9279\,$ | $\,0.9292\,$ | $\,0.9306\,$ | $\,0.9319\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let $X$ denote the length of a handle, and let $Y$ denote the length of a blade. We want to find 

$$
P(150<X+Y<150.5).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(120,0.14)$ and $Y∼N(30,0.02)$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(120+30,0.14+0.02) \\  & ∼N(150,0.16).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =150$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{0.16}=0.4.$

In order to find $P(150<X+Y<150.5),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(150<X+Y<150.5) & =P(\frac{150-150}{0.4}<Z<\frac{150.5-150}{0.4}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<1.25) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.25)-P(Z\le 0) \\  & =Φ(1.25)-Φ(0)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.25) & ≈0.8944,\end{aligned}
$$

and we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0) & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(150<X+Y<150.5) & ≈Φ(1.25)-Φ(0) \\  & ≈0.8944-0.5 \\  & ≈0.3944.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the probability that the length of a randomly selected shovel is more than $150$ centimeters, but less than $150.5$ centimeters is $0.3944.$

$$
