Question 1
?
f(x)∼a02+∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nx) Let F(x)=−5x for x∈[0,π). The Fourier cosine series of the even 2π-periodic extension f(x) of F(x) is shown above. Find the expression for an.an=
10(1−(−1)n)πn2
10(1+(−1)n)πn
10(1−(−1)n)πn2
5(1−(−1)n)4πn
2(1−(−1)n)πn
5(1+(−1)n)πn2
for n≥1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by an=2π∫0πf(x)cos⁡(nx)dx.

In our case, f(x)=−5x for x∈(0,π). So, substituting into the formula, we get an=−10π∫0πxcos⁡(nx)dx.

We use the integration by parts: u=x⇒u′=1v′=cos⁡(nx)⇒v=1nsin⁡(nx)

Thus, we obtain an=−10π(uv|0π−∫0πvu′dx)=−10π(1n[xsin⁡(nx)]0π−1n∫0πsin⁡(nx)dx)=−10nπ((π⋅sin⁡(nπ)−0⋅sin⁡(0))+1n[cos⁡(nx)]0π)=−10nπ(0+1n(cos⁡(nπ)−cos⁡(0)))=10(1−cos⁡(nπ))n2π.

Finally, since cos⁡(nπ)=(−1)n, we have an=10(1−(−1)n)πn2.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-5x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{10}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{10}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{10}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{10}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{10}{n\pi }(0+\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{10(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{10(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

EXPLANATION

For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by an=2π∫0πf(x)cos⁡(nx)dx.

In our case, f(x)=−5x for x∈(0,π). So, substituting into the formula, we get an=−10π∫0πxcos⁡(nx)dx.

We use the integration by parts: u=x⇒u′=1v′=cos⁡(nx)⇒v=1nsin⁡(nx)

Thus, we obtain an=−10π(uv|0π−∫0πvu′dx)=−10π(1n[xsin⁡(nx)]0π−1n∫0πsin⁡(nx)dx)=−10nπ((π⋅sin⁡(nπ)−0⋅sin⁡(0))+1n[cos⁡(nx)]0π)=−10nπ(0+1n(cos⁡(nπ)−cos⁡(0)))=10(1−cos⁡(nπ))n2π.

Finally, since cos⁡(nπ)=(−1)n, we have an=10(1−(−1)n)πn2.

solution.reasoning: For the even extension, a_n=(2/\pi)\int_0^\pi(-5x)\cos(nx)\,dx. Integration by parts gives \int_0^\pi x\cos(nx)\,dx= ((-1)^n-1)/n^2, so a_n=10(1-(-1)^n)/(\pi n^2), which is option 1. The mathematics is conclusive, but no Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence is captured.

feedback.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=-5x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{n}.$

$\,{a}_{n}=$ {{field-1}}
for $n\ge 1$
feedback.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-5x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{10}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{10}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{10}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{10}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{10}{n\pi }(0+\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{10(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{10(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{0}.$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{[3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{3})]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{3}{2}-3) \\  & =-\frac{3}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Let $F(x)=3x+1$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼(1+\frac{3}{2}\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
question.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=3x+1$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(3x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3x+1\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=3 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(3x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{3}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((3\pi +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{3}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0+\frac{3}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-1)}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{6((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(1+\frac{3}{2}\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

Question 3
?
Let F(x)=3x+1 for x∈[0,π). Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the even 2π-periodic extension f(x) of the function F(x) below.
6((−1)n−1)πn2
3(−1)nπn
3(1−(−1)n)πn
6(−1)nπn2
6((−1)n−1)πn2
cos⁡(nx)
cos⁡(πx)
sin⁡(πx)
sin⁡(nx)
cos⁡(nx)
f(x)∼(1+32π)+∑n=1∞{(3(−1)nπn)(S0)}⋅{(cos⁡(πx))(S1)}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by an=2π∫0πf(x)cos⁡(nx)dx.

In our case, f(x)=3x+1 for x∈(0,π). So, substituting into the formula, we get an=2π∫0π(3x+1)cos⁡(nx)dx.

We use the integration by parts: u=3x+1⇒u′=3v′=cos⁡(nx)⇒v=1nsin⁡(nx)

Thus, we obtain an=2π(uv|0π−∫0πvu′dx)=2π(1n[(3x+1)sin⁡(nx)]0π−3n∫0πsin⁡(nx)dx)=2nπ(((3π+1)sin⁡(nπ)−sin⁡(0))+3n[cos⁡(nx)]0π)=2nπ(0+3n(cos⁡(nπ)−cos⁡(0)))=6(cos⁡(nπ)−1)n2π.

Therefore, since cos⁡(nπ)=(−1)n, we have an=6((−1)n−1)πn2.

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is f(x)∼(1+32π)+∑n=1∞6((−1)n−1)πn2⋅cos⁡(nx).

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=3x+1$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(3x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3x+1\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=3 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(3x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{3}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((3\pi +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{3}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0+\frac{3}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-1)}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{6((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(1+\frac{3}{2}\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

question.problem:

$$
f(x)∼(1+\frac{3}{2}\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$

Question 3

Let F(x)=3x+1 for x∈[0,π). Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the even 2π-periodic extension f(x) of the function F(x) below.
6((−1)n−1)πn2
3(−1)nπn
3(1−(−1)n)πn
6(−1)nπn2
6((−1)n−1)πn2
cos⁡(nx)
cos⁡(πx)
sin⁡(πx)
sin⁡(nx)
cos⁡(nx)
f(x)∼(1+32π)+∑n=1∞{(3(−1)nπn)(S0)}⋅{(cos⁡(πx))(S1)}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by an=2π∫0πf(x)cos⁡(nx)dx.

In our case, f(x)=3x+1 for x∈(0,π). So, substituting into the formula, we get an=2π∫0π(3x+1)cos⁡(nx)dx.

We use the integration by parts: u=3x+1⇒u′=3v′=cos⁡(nx)⇒v=1nsin⁡(nx)

Thus, we obtain an=2π(uv|0π−∫0πvu′dx)=2π(1n[(3x+1)sin⁡(nx)]0π−3n∫0πsin⁡(nx)dx)=2nπ(((3π+1)sin⁡(nπ)−sin⁡(0))+3n[cos⁡(nx)]0π)=2nπ(0+3n(cos⁡(nπ)−cos⁡(0)))=6(cos⁡(nπ)−1)n2π.

Therefore, since cos⁡(nπ)=(−1)n, we have an=6((−1)n−1)πn2.

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is f(x)∼(1+32π)+∑n=1∞6((−1)n−1)πn2⋅cos⁡(nx).

solution.reasoning: The even extension has cosine terms cos(nx). For n≥1, a_n=(2/\pi)\int_0^\pi(3x+1)\cos(nx)\,dx=6((-1)^n-1)/(\pi n^2), since the constant term integrates to zero and \int_0^\pi x\cos(nx)\,dx=((-1)^n-1)/n^2. The constant coefficient a_0/2=1+3\pi/2 also matches the displayed series. Both fields therefore use option 3. No Math Academy answer or grading evidence is captured.

feedback.problem:
Let $F(x)=3x+1$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼(1+\frac{3}{2}\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=3x+1$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(3x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3x+1\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=3 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(3x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{3}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((3\pi +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{3}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0+\frac{3}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-1)}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{6((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(1+\frac{3}{2}\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=8{x}^{2}+3$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{0}.$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=8{x}^{2}+3$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(8{x}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{[\frac{8{x}^{3}}{3}+3x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{8{\pi }^{3}}{3}+3\pi )-0 \\  & =2(\frac{8{\pi }^{2}}{3}+3).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $4$ and $2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 11\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $12$ and $2.$

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 11\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $3$ and $5.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $17$ and $7.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=17$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=7.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-7I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-7I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1$ and $6.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-6I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $5,$ $3,$ and $2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3,\,{\lambda }_{3}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{3}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1,$ $3,$ and $9.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=9,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 4 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{3}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $10,$ $5,$ and $3.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=10,\,{\lambda }_{2}=5,\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-5I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $5,$ $4,$ and $2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1,$ $4,$ and $8.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=8,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{6},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/7839eb7b2cfa2511661a6f2822930cd54ef4c3f2cb7df53448af61bdb7f63766.svg)
Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $16$ and $6.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
\lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \cdots\gt \lambda_n
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_1$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue $\lambda_1,$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_2$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue $\lambda_2,$

- $\cdots$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are $\lambda_1=16$ and $\lambda_2=6.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2=6{:}$

Applying our usual algorithm for finding eigenvectors, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}C-6I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 3 & 15\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/e5ce684566df94e2d3691bb3fd75b78e46bbfe20bc3ed037618175c619cbe89a.svg) 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/10818d19ffec73c77257977086f97924f8c3ff35fdb4cb46a1a84fa243bbcdbb.svg) 

Therefore, the second principal component of the data is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/3cfd9b938a757c8e5b06ebf426b71e0439175e862da98ac7e65e74ee413f2d68.svg)

                    Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/f51f3460981ca243627f1873a24fa3a50a43275bebdb20c1ced5d64215c71618.svg)
Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $S$ are $8,$ $5,$ and $2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
\lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \cdots\gt \lambda_n
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector $u_1$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue $\lambda_1,$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector $u_2$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue $\lambda_2,$

- $\cdots$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
\lambda_1=8,\qquad
\lambda_2=5,\qquad
\lambda_3=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=8{:}$

Applying our usual algorithm for finding eigenvectors, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}C-8I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-8I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/eb25f50c2550e470fcdffd1c94a5ff2134043ac34b6a75b14e2ce00d1936a2e8.svg) 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| =3,$ we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/920ccfb9953cf4e17f89b01a1f5512f8c0bbcc368f9af1770f768c1e258127e5.svg) 

Therefore, the first principal component of the data is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/0c20bbbce9a9014103e94d0f8b055f6dfec18672f2b313d46b1799d9402f755a.svg)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that the principal components of a standardized observation matrix $X$ are the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$ If 

$$
\lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \cdots\gt \lambda_n
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_1$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue $\lambda_1,$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_2$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue $\lambda_2,$

- $\cdots$

and so on.

For example, suppose that the covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/e40cd1a0df89ba171b921ab971e8eee25e284265df13b7e031ea32fc28d2c27b.svg)

It's easy to show that the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
\lambda_1=10, \qquad
\lambda_2=8.
$$

To find the first principal component of the data, we need the unit eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=10.$ 

Applying our usual algorithm for finding eigenvectors, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}C-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 1 \\ 1 & 9\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/c7050bbb395b939b1b0559b3e7515c4be4f572aed61090f1a4489e126763240f.svg) 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/7b0a41deb385aa2471cae701c9f87938085256879a8d834535f8ec0e3f431f27.svg) 

Therefore, the $1$st principal component of the data is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/9490f2e5105592fa3976ae506cbdf64d70c3372d1cc9295eaa6c6580a4ac75aa.svg)

**Note:** The opposite vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/e2b366cfb8cb5b708eb5ba443dfc61c05b498d4eb737b375c8ebc86b96e8eea6.svg) also works in the example above.

Recall that the principal components of a standardized observation matrix $X$ are the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$ If 

$$
\lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \cdots\gt \lambda_n
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_1$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue $\lambda_1,$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_2$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue $\lambda_2,$

- $\cdots$

and so on.

For example, suppose that the covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/e40cd1a0df89ba171b921ab971e8eee25e284265df13b7e031ea32fc28d2c27b.svg)

It's easy to show that the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
\lambda_1=10, \qquad
\lambda_2=8.
$$

To find the first principal component of the data, we need the unit eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=10.$ 

Applying our usual algorithm for finding eigenvectors, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}C-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 1 \\ 1 & 9\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/c7050bbb395b939b1b0559b3e7515c4be4f572aed61090f1a4489e126763240f.svg) 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/7b0a41deb385aa2471cae701c9f87938085256879a8d834535f8ec0e3f431f27.svg) 

Therefore, the $1$st principal component of the data is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/9490f2e5105592fa3976ae506cbdf64d70c3372d1cc9295eaa6c6580a4ac75aa.svg)

**Note:** The opposite vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/e2b366cfb8cb5b708eb5ba443dfc61c05b498d4eb737b375c8ebc86b96e8eea6.svg) also works in the example above.

tutorial.content:
Recall that the principal components of a standardized observation matrix $X$ are the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$ If 

$$
\lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \cdots\gt \lambda_n
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_1$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue $\lambda_1,$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_2$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue $\lambda_2,$

- $\cdots$

and so on.

For example, suppose that the covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/86cd114656be47342171ec85d1a597e98403f7b4bcd40e8eca9a48cf5c484c21.svg)

It's easy to show that the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
\lambda_1=10, \qquad
\lambda_2=8.
$$

To find the first principal component of the data, we need the unit eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=10.$ 

Applying our usual algorithm for finding eigenvectors, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}C-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 1 \\ 1 & 9\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/9609698d9ffecd2d7afceaa6c3bc343a737819f9b5bf6a1e77cc31c887233ad5.svg) 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/4eb734f1c0bc45ec8298850310816343c9b8d5da765c1b38dea8b18f192d299d.svg) 

Therefore, the $1$st principal component of the data is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/4f503d9e84c83f8b4409df389ae8f814dbbb91f27385534b0b0d8b06d004926b.svg)

**Note:** The opposite vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/1674dcbe0ef0bffa803460fc8939c915aa22aba9f8195cb5842f177d63b76f0c.svg) also works in the example above.

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $4$ and $2.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[3−1−13] Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 4 and 2.

a
15[1−2]
b
15[12]
c
[11]
d
12[11]
e
12[1−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=4 and λ2=2. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=4:

C−4I=[3−1−13]−4[1001]=[−1−1−1−1]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[1−1].

Finally, dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[1−1].

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=12$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 11\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 11\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $12$ and $2.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=12$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 11\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[33311] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 12 and 2.

a
113[−32]
b
 113[−23]
c
110[31]
d
 110[−31]
e
 [10]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=12 and λ2=2. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=2:

C−2I=[33311]−2[1001]=[1339]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−31].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=10, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=110[−31].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$

$$

Question 5

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[2−2−25] Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 1 and 6.

a
15[12]
b
15[1−2]
c
12[11]
d
13[12]
e
15[21]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=6 and λ2=1. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=6:

C−6I=[2−2−25]−6[1001]=[−4−2−2−1]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−6I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[1−2].

Finally, dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get

v1‖v1‖=15[1−2].

observed_steps.name: Question 6
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3,\,{\lambda }_{3}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{3}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $5,$ $3,$ and $2.$

question.html:
Question 6
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[401020104] Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 5, 3, and 2.

a
 [010]
b
15[102]
c
13[11−1]
d
 16[1−21]
e
12[−101]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=5,λ2=3,λ3=2.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ3=2:

C−2I=[401020104]−2[100010001]=[201000102].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[010].

Finally, dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=1, we get

u3=v3‖v3‖=[010].

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=9,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 4 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{3}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$

$$

Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1,$ $3,$ and $9.$

question.html:
Question 7
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[4−2−3−252−324] Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 1, 3, and 9.

a
 12[110]
b
 12[101]
c
 12[−101]
d
 12[0−11]
e
 12[011]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=9,λ2=3,λ3=1.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ3=1:

C−I=[4−2−3−252−324]−[100010001]=[3−2−3−242−323].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[101].

Finally, dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=2, we get

u3=v3‖v3‖=12[101].

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=10,\,{\lambda }_{2}=5,\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-5I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $10,$ $5,$ and $3.$

$$

$$

$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-5I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 8
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[300092026] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 10, 5, and 3.

a
12[−110]
b
13[1−11]
c
15[201]
d
12[101]
e
15[0−12]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=10,λ2=5,λ3=3.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=5:

C−5I=[300092026]−5[100010001]=[−200042021].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−5I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[0−12].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=15[0−12].

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $5,$ $4,$ and $2.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[311140104] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 5, 4, and 2.

a
13[1−11]
b
12[101]
c
12[0−11]
d
13[21−2]
e
111[131]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ3,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=5,λ2=4,λ2=2.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=4:

C−4I=[311140104]−4[100010001]=[−111100100].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[0−11].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=12[0−11].

observed_steps.name: Question 10
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=8,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{6},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1,$ $4,$ and $8.$

$$

$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 10
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[31−1153−135] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 1, 4, and 8.

a
 16[2−11]
b
 16[21−1]
c
 16[211]
d
 16[12−1]
e
 16[−112]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=8,λ2=4,λ3=1.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=4:

C−4I=[31−1153−135]−4[100010001]=[−11−1113−131].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[21−1].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=6, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=16[21−1].

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $4$ and $2.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[3−1−13] Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 4 and 2.

a
15[1−2]
b
15[12]
c
[11]
d
12[11]
e
12[1−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=4 and λ2=2. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=4:

C−4I=[3−1−13]−4[1001]=[−1−1−1−1]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[1−1].

Finally, dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[1−1].

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $4$ and $2.$

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[3−1−13] Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 4 and 2.

a
15[1−2]
b
15[12]
c
[11]
d
12[11]
e
12[1−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=4 and λ2=2. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=4:

C−4I=[3−1−13]−4[1001]=[−1−1−1−1]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[1−1].

Finally, dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[1−1].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix

solution.reasoning: The first principal component corresponds to the largest eigenvalue, 4. Solving (C-4I)v=0 gives x+y=0, so (1,-1) is an eigenvector. Its norm is \sqrt{2}, yielding option e. The opposite unit vector is equivalent. No answer key or grade for this current question is captured; the worked example concerns a different matrix.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $4$ and $2.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

feedback.html:
Question 1
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[3−1−13] Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 4 and 2.

a
15[1−2]
b
15[12]
c
[11]
d
12[11]
e
12[1−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=4 and λ2=2. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=4:

C−4I=[3−1−13]−4[1001]=[−1−1−1−1]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[1−1].

Finally, dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[1−1].
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 11\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $12$ and $2.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=12$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 11\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[33311] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 12 and 2.

a
113[−32]
b
 113[−23]
c
110[31]
d
 110[−31]
e
 [10]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=12 and λ2=2. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=2:

C−2I=[33311]−2[1001]=[1339]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−31].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=10, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=110[−31].

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=12$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 11\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
