question.html:
Question 2
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[33311] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 12 and 2.

a
113[−32]
b
 113[−23]
c
110[31]
d
 110[−31]
e
 [10]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=12 and λ2=2. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=2:

C−2I=[33311]−2[1001]=[1339]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−31].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=10, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=110[−31].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix

solution.reasoning: The second principal component corresponds to the smaller eigenvalue, 2. Solving (C-2I)v=0 gives x+3y=0, so (-3,1) is an eigenvector. Dividing by its norm, \sqrt{10}, yields option d. Its negative is equally valid. The provided worked example uses a different matrix; no Math Academy answer or grade is captured for this question.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 11\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $12$ and $2.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=12$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 11\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 2
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[33311] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 12 and 2.

a
113[−32]
b
 113[−23]
c
110[31]
d
 110[−31]
e
 [10]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=12 and λ2=2. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=2:

C−2I=[33311]−2[1001]=[1339]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−31].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=10, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=110[−31].

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $3$ and $5.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[4−1−14] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 3 and 5.

a
15[2−1]
b
12[11]
c
15[21]
d
15[12]
e
12[−11]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=5 and λ2=3. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=3:

C−3I=[4−1−14]−3[1001]=[1−1−11]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−3I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[11].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=12[11].

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

\begin{aligned}C-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[4−1−14] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 3 and 5.

a
15[2−1]
b
12[11]
c
15[21]
d
15[12]
e
12[−11]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=5 and λ2=3. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=3:

C−3I=[4−1−14]−3[1001]=[1−1−11]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−3I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[11].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=12[11].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix

solution.reasoning: Order the eigenvalues as 5 > 3. The second principal component corresponds to 3. Solving (C-3I)v=0 gives x-y=0, so (1,1) is an eigenvector. Its norm is \sqrt{2}, giving option b. feedback.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $3$ and $5.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 3
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[4−1−14] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 3 and 5.

a
15[2−1]
b
12[11]
c
15[21]
d
15[12]
e
12[−11]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=5 and λ2=3. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=3:

C−3I=[4−1−14]−3[1001]=[1−1−11]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−3I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[11].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=12[11].
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $17$ and $7.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=17$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=7.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-7I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-7I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[83316] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 17 and 7.

a
110[−31]
b
110[13]
c
15[−21]
d
12[−11]
e
15[12]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=17 and λ2=7. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=7:

C−7I=[83316]−7[1001]=[1339]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−7I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−31].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=10, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=110[−31].

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=17$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=7.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-7I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-7I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $17$ and $7.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=17$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=7.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-7I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-7I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1$ and $6.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-6I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[2−2−25] Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 1 and 6.

a
15[12]
b
15[1−2]
c
12[11]
d
13[12]
e
15[21]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=6 and λ2=1. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=6:

C−6I=[2−2−25]−6[1001]=[−4−2−2−1]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−6I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[1−2].

Finally, dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get

v1‖v1‖=15[1−2].

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-6I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1$ and $6.$

Question 5
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[2−2−25] Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 1 and 6.

a
15[12]
b
15[1−2]
c
12[11]
d
13[12]
e
15[21]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are λ1=6 and λ2=1. So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=6:

C−6I=[2−2−25]−6[1001]=[−4−2−2−1]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−6I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[1−2].

Finally, dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get

v1‖v1‖=15[1−2].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Principal Component Given a 2x2 Covariance Matrix

solution.reasoning: The first principal component corresponds to the largest eigenvalue, 6. Solving (C-6I)v=0 gives -4x-2y=0, hence y=-2x. The eigenvector (1,-2) has norm \sqrt{5}, so its normalization is option b. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different matrix.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1$ and $6.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-6I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

C−6I=[2−2−25]−6[1001]=[−4−2−2−1]

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−6I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[1−2].

Finally, dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get

v1‖v1‖=15[1−2].

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $5,$ $3,$ and $2.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3,\,{\lambda }_{3}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{3}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

λ1=5,λ2=3,λ3=2.

C−2I=[401020104]−2[100010001]=[201000102].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[010].

Finally, dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=1, we get

u3=v3‖v3‖=[010].

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3,\,{\lambda }_{3}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{3}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $5,$ $3,$ and $2.$

$$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

$$

\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 6
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[401020104] Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 5, 3, and 2.

a
 [010]
b
15[102]
c
13[11−1]
d
 16[1−21]
e
12[−101]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=5,λ2=3,λ3=2.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ3=2:

C−2I=[401020104]−2[100010001]=[201000102].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[010].

Finally, dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=1, we get

u3=v3‖v3‖=[010].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix

solution.reasoning: The third principal component corresponds to the smallest eigenvalue, 2. Solving (C-2I)v=0 gives 2x+z=0 and x+2z=0, implying x=z=0 while y is free. Thus (0,1,0) is a unit eigenvector, giving option a. No Math Academy answer key or grade is captured for this question; the worked example concerns a different matrix.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $5,$ $3,$ and $2.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3,\,{\lambda }_{3}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{3}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 6
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[401020104] Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 5, 3, and 2.

a
 [010]
b
15[102]
c
13[11−1]
d
 16[1−21]
e
12[−101]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=5,λ2=3,λ3=2.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ3=2:

C−2I=[401020104]−2[100010001]=[201000102].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[010].

Finally, dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=1, we get

u3=v3‖v3‖=[010].

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1,$ $3,$ and $9.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=9,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 4 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{3}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[4−2−3−252−324] Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 1, 3, and 9.

a
 12[110]
b
 12[101]
c
 12[−101]
d
 12[0−11]
e
 12[011]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=9,λ2=3,λ3=1.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ3=1:

C−I=[4−2−3−252−324]−[100010001]=[3−2−3−242−323].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[101].

Finally, dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=2, we get

u3=v3‖v3‖=12[101].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix

last_observation.name: Question 7
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=9,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 4 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{3}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.problem:

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1,$ $3,$ and $9.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=9,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -3 \\ -2 & 4 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{3}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $10,$ $5,$ and $3.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=10,\,{\lambda }_{2}=5,\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-5I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[300092026] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 10, 5, and 3.

a
12[−110]
b
13[1−11]
c
15[201]
d
12[101]
e
15[0−12]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=10,λ2=5,λ3=3.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=5:

C−5I=[300092026]−5[100010001]=[−200042021].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−5I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[0−12].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=15[0−12].

last_observation.name: Question 8
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=10,\,{\lambda }_{2}=5,\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-5I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $10,$ $5,$ and $3.$

question.html:
Question 8
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[300092026] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 10, 5, and 3.

a
12[−110]
b
13[1−11]
c
15[201]
d
12[101]
e
15[0−12]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=10,λ2=5,λ3=3.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=5:

C−5I=[300092026]−5[100010001]=[−200042021].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−5I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[0−12].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=15[0−12].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix

solution.reasoning: The second principal component corresponds to eigenvalue 5, since 10 > 5 > 3. Solving (C-5I)v=0 gives x=0 and 4y+2z=0, hence z=-2y. Thus (0,-1,2) is an eigenvector with norm \sqrt{5}, yielding option e after normalization. No Math Academy answer key or grade is captured for this question; the supplied worked example concerns a different matrix.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $10,$ $5,$ and $3.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=10,\,{\lambda }_{2}=5,\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-5I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 8
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[300092026] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 10, 5, and 3.

a
12[−110]
b
13[1−11]
c
15[201]
d
12[101]
e
15[0−12]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=10,λ2=5,λ3=3.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=5:

C−5I=[300092026]−5[100010001]=[−200042021].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−5I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[0−12].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=15[0−12].

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $5,$ $4,$ and $2.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[311140104] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 5, 4, and 2.

a
13[1−11]
b
12[101]
c
12[0−11]
d
13[21−2]
e
111[131]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ3,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=5,λ2=4,λ2=2.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=4:

C−4I=[311140104]−4[100010001]=[−111100100].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[0−11].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=12[0−11].

last_observation.name: Question 9
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $5,$ $4,$ and $2.$

Question 9
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[311140104] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 5, 4, and 2.

a
13[1−11]
b
12[101]
c
12[0−11]
d
13[21−2]
e
111[131]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ3,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=5,λ2=4,λ2=2.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=4:

C−4I=[311140104]−4[100010001]=[−111100100].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[0−11].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=12[0−11].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix

solution.reasoning: The second principal component corresponds to eigenvalue 4, since 5 > 4 > 2. Solving (C-4I)v=0 gives x=0 and y+z=0. Thus (0,-1,1) is an eigenvector with norm \sqrt{2}, yielding option c after normalization. feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $5,$ $4,$ and $2.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1,$ $4,$ and $8.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=8,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{6},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

last_observation.name: Question 10
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=8,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{6},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1,$ $4,$ and $8.$

question.html:
Question 10
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[31−1153−135] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 1, 4, and 8.

a
 16[2−11]
b
 16[21−1]
c
 16[211]
d
 16[12−1]
e
 16[−112]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=8,λ2=4,λ3=1.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=4:

C−4I=[31−1153−135]−4[100010001]=[−11−1113−131].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[21−1].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=6, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=16[21−1].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Principal Component Given a 3x3 Covariance Matrix

solution.reasoning: Order the eigenvalues as 8 > 4 > 1. The second principal component corresponds to 4. Solving (C-4I)v=0 gives x=2y and z=-y, so (2,1,-1) is an eigenvector. Its norm is \sqrt{6}, yielding option b after normalization. No Math Academy answer key or grade is captured for this question; the worked example concerns a different matrix.

feedback.name: Question 10
feedback.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1,$ $4,$ and $8.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=8,\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{6},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

feedback.html:
Question 10
?

The covariance matrix C of some particular observations is shown below. C=[31−1153−135] Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of C are 1, 4, and 8.

a
 16[2−11]
b
 16[21−1]
c
 16[211]
d
 16[12−1]
e
 16[−112]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C are called the principal components of the data. If

λ1>λ2>⋯>λn

are the eigenvalues of C written in descending order, then:

  • the 1st principal component is the unit eigenvector u1 corresponding to the 1st eigenvalue λ1,

  • the 2nd principal component is the unit eigenvector u2 corresponding to the 2nd eigenvalue λ2,

  • ⋯

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix C, in descending order, are

λ1=8,λ2=4,λ3=1.

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ2=4:

C−4I=[31−1153−135]−4[100010001]=[−11−1113−131].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (C−4I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[21−1].

Finally, dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=6, we get

u2=v2‖v2‖=16[21−1].

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,k \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+z\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz))\text{ }j+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})\,i+(-(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})+0\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0))\,j+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0)\,k \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

5.Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient?

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface x=y2−z2 at the point (3,2,1).

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the plane curve xy=x2+y2−7. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (2,−1).

a
−x−3y+5=0
b
3x−5y+1=0
c
−2x−2y+3=0
d
−5x−4y+1=0
e
4x+5y−3=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: xy=x2+y2−70=x2+y2−xy−7

If we set f(x,y)=x2+y2−xy−7, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=0.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (2,−1) can be found by computing ∇f(2,−1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (2,−1):

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(x2+y2−xy−7)i+∂∂y(x2+y2−xy−7)j=(2x−y)i+(2y−x)j∇f(2,−1)=(2(2)−(−1))i+(2(−1)−2)j=5i−4j=⟨5,−4⟩

Hence, ∇f(2,−1)=⟨5,−4⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (2,−1).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−25=y−(−1)−4−4(x−2)=5(y+1)−4x−5y+8−5=0−4x−5y+3=04x+5y−3=0

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$
question.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

For the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0).

a
i+j
b
35i+45j+k
c
45i+35j
d
35i+45j+15k
e
35i+45j
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0) can be found by computing ∇f(3,4,0).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(3,4,0):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x2+y2+z2)i+∂∂y(x2+y2+z2)j+∂∂z(x2+y2+z2)k=xx2+y2+z2 i+yx2+y2+z2 j+zx2+y2+z2 k∇f(3,4,0)=3(3)2+(4)2+(0)2i+4(3)2+(4)2+(0)2j+0(3)2+(4)2+(0)2k=35i+45j

Therefore, 35i+45j is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0).

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the plane curve x2−3y2=6. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (3,1).

a
x−3y=0
b
 x−y−2=0
c
x+3y−6=0
d
 x+y−4=0
e
2x+y−7=0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If we set f(x,y)=x2−3y2, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=6.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (3,1) can be found by computing ∇f(3,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (3,1): ∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(x2−3y2)i+∂∂y(x2−3y2)j=2xi−6yj∇f(3,1)=2(3)i−6(1)j=6i−6j=⟨6,−6⟩

Hence, ∇f(3,1)=⟨6,−6⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (3,1).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as: x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−36=y−1(−6)−6(x−3)=6(y−1)−(x−3)=y−1−x+3=y−1x+y−4=0

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface x=y2−z2 at the point (3,2,1).

a
 x−3=y−22=z−1
b
 x−3=2−y4=z−12
c
 x−32=y−24=z−1
d
 x−14=2−y=z−1
e
x−1=y−2=z−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: x=y2−z2y2−z2−x=0

If we set f(x,y,z)=y2−z2−x, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (3,2,1) can be found by computing ∇f(3,2,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (3,2,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(y2−z2−x)i+∂∂y(y2−z2−x)j+∂∂z(y2−z2−x)k=−i+2yj−2zk∇f(3,2,1)=−i+2(2)j−2(1)k=−i+4j−2k=⟨−1,4,−2⟩

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0,z0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vzx−3(−1)=y−24=z−1(−2)x−31=y−2−4=z−12x−3=2−y4=z−12

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$
