last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the plane curve xy=x2+y2−7. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (2,−1).

a
−x−3y+5=0
b
3x−5y+1=0
c
−2x−2y+3=0
d
−5x−4y+1=0
e
4x+5y−3=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: xy=x2+y2−70=x2+y2−xy−7

If we set f(x,y)=x2+y2−xy−7, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=0.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (2,−1) can be found by computing ∇f(2,−1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (2,−1):

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(x2+y2−xy−7)i+∂∂y(x2+y2−xy−7)j=(2x−y)i+(2y−x)j∇f(2,−1)=(2(2)−(−1))i+(2(−1)−2)j=5i−4j=⟨5,−4⟩

Hence, ∇f(2,−1)=⟨5,−4⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (2,−1).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−25=y−(−1)−4−4(x−2)=5(y+1)−4x−5y+8−5=0−4x−5y+3=04x+5y−3=0

solution.reasoning: Implicit differentiation gives y+xy'=2x+2yy', so y'=(2x-y)/(x-2y). At (2,-1), the tangent slope is 5/4, hence the normal slope is -4/5. Thus y+1=-(4/5)(x-2), equivalent to 4x+5y-3=0, choice e. Mathematical correctness is established, but no Math Academy answer-key evidence was captured.

Consider the plane curve xy=x2+y2−7. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (2,−1).

a
−x−3y+5=0
b
3x−5y+1=0
c
−2x−2y+3=0
d
−5x−4y+1=0
e
4x+5y−3=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: xy=x2+y2−70=x2+y2−xy−7

If we set f(x,y)=x2+y2−xy−7, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=0.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (2,−1) can be found by computing ∇f(2,−1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (2,−1):

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(x2+y2−xy−7)i+∂∂y(x2+y2−xy−7)j=(2x−y)i+(2y−x)j∇f(2,−1)=(2(2)−(−1))i+(2(−1)−2)j=5i−4j=⟨5,−4⟩

Hence, ∇f(2,−1)=⟨5,−4⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (2,−1).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−25=y−(−1)−4−4(x−2)=5(y+1)−4x−5y+8−5=0−4x−5y+3=04x+5y−3=0

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$
question.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

question.html:
Question 2
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0).

a
i+j
b
35i+45j+k
c
45i+35j
d
35i+45j+15k
e
35i+45j
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0) can be found by computing ∇f(3,4,0).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(3,4,0):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x2+y2+z2)i+∂∂y(x2+y2+z2)j+∂∂z(x2+y2+z2)k=xx2+y2+z2 i+yx2+y2+z2 j+zx2+y2+z2 k∇f(3,4,0)=3(3)2+(4)2+(0)2i+4(3)2+(4)2+(0)2j+0(3)2+(4)2+(0)2k=35i+45j

Therefore, 35i+45j is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0).

last_observation.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

question.html:
Question 2
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0).

a
i+j
b
35i+45j+k
c
45i+35j
d
35i+45j+15k
e
35i+45j
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0) can be found by computing ∇f(3,4,0).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(3,4,0):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x2+y2+z2)i+∂∂y(x2+y2+z2)j+∂∂z(x2+y2+z2)k=xx2+y2+z2 i+yx2+y2+z2 j+zx2+y2+z2 k∇f(3,4,0)=3(3)2+(4)2+(0)2i+4(3)2+(4)2+(0)2j+0(3)2+(4)2+(0)2k=35i+45j

Therefore, 35i+45j is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0).

solution.reasoning: The gradient is perpendicular to a level surface: \nabla f=(x,y,z)/\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}. At (3,4,0), this is (3/5,4/5,0), so choice e is correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$
feedback.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$
question.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,k \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+z\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz))\text{ }j+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})\,i+(-(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})+0\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0))\,j+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0)\,k \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$

Question 3
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=cos⁡(xy)+sin⁡(yz), find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,π2,0).

a
−π2i−j+π2k
b
−π2i
c
−π2i+π2k
d
−j+π2k
e
−π2i−j
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,π2,0) can be found by computing ∇f(1,π2,0).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(1,π2,0):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(cos⁡(xy)+sin⁡(yz))i+∂∂y(cos⁡(xy)+sin⁡(yz))j+∂∂z(cos⁡(xy)+sin⁡(yz))k=−ysin⁡(xy) i+(−xsin⁡(xy)+zcos⁡(yz)) j+ycos⁡(yz) k∇f(1,π2,0)=−π2sin⁡(1⋅π2)i+(−(1)sin⁡(1⋅π2)+0cos⁡(π2⋅0))j+π2cos⁡(π2⋅0)k=−π2i−j+π2k

Therefore, −π2i−j+π2k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,π2,0).

last_observation.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,k \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+z\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz))\text{ }j+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})\,i+(-(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})+0\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0))\,j+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0)\,k \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$
question.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the plane curve x2−3y2=6. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (3,1).

a
x−3y=0
b
 x−y−2=0
c
x+3y−6=0
d
 x+y−4=0
e
2x+y−7=0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If we set f(x,y)=x2−3y2, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=6.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (3,1) can be found by computing ∇f(3,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (3,1): ∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(x2−3y2)i+∂∂y(x2−3y2)j=2xi−6yj∇f(3,1)=2(3)i−6(1)j=6i−6j=⟨6,−6⟩

Hence, ∇f(3,1)=⟨6,−6⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (3,1).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as: x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−36=y−1(−6)−6(x−3)=6(y−1)−(x−3)=y−1−x+3=y−1x+y−4=0

last_observation.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface x=y2−z2 at the point (3,2,1).

a
 x−3=y−22=z−1
b
 x−3=2−y4=z−12
c
 x−32=y−24=z−1
d
 x−14=2−y=z−1
e
x−1=y−2=z−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: x=y2−z2y2−z2−x=0

If we set f(x,y,z)=y2−z2−x, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (3,2,1) can be found by computing ∇f(3,2,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (3,2,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(y2−z2−x)i+∂∂y(y2−z2−x)j+∂∂z(y2−z2−x)k=−i+2yj−2zk∇f(3,2,1)=−i+2(2)j−2(1)k=−i+4j−2k=⟨−1,4,−2⟩

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0,z0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vzx−3(−1)=y−24=z−1(−2)x−31=y−2−4=z−12x−3=2−y4=z−12

solution.reasoning: Write the surface as F(x,y,z)=x-y^2+z^2=0. Its gradient at (3,2,1) is (1,-4,2), a normal direction. The normal line is (x,y,z)=(3,2,1)+t(1,-4,2), giving x-3=(2-y)/4=(z-1)/2, choice b. No captured Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence is supplied.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface x=y2−z2 at the point (3,2,1).

a
 x−3=y−22=z−1
b
 x−3=2−y4=z−12
c
 x−32=y−24=z−1
d
 x−14=2−y=z−1
e
x−1=y−2=z−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: x=y2−z2y2−z2−x=0

If we set f(x,y,z)=y2−z2−x, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (3,2,1) can be found by computing ∇f(3,2,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (3,2,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(y2−z2−x)i+∂∂y(y2−z2−x)j+∂∂z(y2−z2−x)k=−i+2yj−2zk∇f(3,2,1)=−i+2(2)j−2(1)k=−i+4j−2k=⟨−1,4,−2⟩

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0,z0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vzx−3(−1)=y−24=z−1(−2)x−31=y−2−4=z−12x−3=2−y4=z−12

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
Given the complex number $a+b\,\text{i},$ $a$ represents its real part while $b$ represents its imaginary part.

To add or subtract complex numbers, we add or subtract their real parts, and we add or subtract their imaginary parts.

For the given problem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(7+10\,\text{i})+(5+3\,\text{i}) & =(7+5)+(10+3)\,\text{i} \\  & =12+13\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To add complex numbers, we just add the real parts and add the imaginary parts separately. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}(3+5\text{i})+(2-3\text{i}) & =(3+5\text{i})+(2-3\text{i}) \\  & =(3+2)+(5+(-\,3))\text{i} \\  & =(3+2)+(5-3)\text{i} \\  & =5+2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we write

$$
(a + b\textrm{i}) + (c + d\textrm{i}) = (a + c) + (b + d)\textrm{i}.
$$

Subtracting complex numbers works in the same way: we just subtract the real parts and subtract the imaginary parts separately. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}(3+5\text{i})-(2-3\text{i}) & =(3+5\text{i})-(2-3\text{i}) \\  & =(3-2)+(5-(-\,3))\text{i} \\  & =(3-2)+(5+3)\text{i} \\  & =1+8\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we write

$$
(a + b\textrm{i}) - (c + d\textrm{i}) = (a - c) + (b - d)\textrm{i}.
$$

question.problem:

{{field-1}}$-\,$

question.worked_solution:
Given the complex number $a+b\,\text{i},$ $a$ represents its real part while $b$ represents its imaginary part.

To add or subtract complex numbers, we add or subtract their real parts, and we add or subtract their imaginary parts.

For the given problem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(11-\sqrt{-80})-(6+\sqrt{-125}) & =(11-\sqrt{16\cdot 5}\,\text{i})-(6+\sqrt{25\cdot 5}\,\text{i}) \\  & =(11-4\sqrt{5}\,\text{i})-(6+5\sqrt{5}\,\text{i}) \\  & =(11-6)+(-4\sqrt{5}-5\sqrt{5})\,\text{i} \\  & =5-9\sqrt{5}\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:

question.worked_solution:
Given the complex number $a+b\,\text{i},$ $a$ represents its real part while $b$ represents its imaginary part.

To add or subtract complex numbers, we add or subtract their real parts, and we add or subtract their imaginary parts.

For the given problem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(1+\sqrt{-45})-(-5+\sqrt{-20}) & =(1+\sqrt{9\cdot 5}\,\text{i})-(-5+\sqrt{4\cdot 5}\,\text{i}) \\  & =(1+3\sqrt{5}\,\text{i})-(-5+2\sqrt{5}\,\text{i}) \\  & =(1-(-5))+(3\sqrt{5}-2\sqrt{5})\,\text{i} \\  & =(1+5)+\sqrt{5}\,\text{i} \\  & =6+\sqrt{5}\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

To add or subtract complex numbers, we add or subtract their real parts, and we add or subtract their imaginary parts.

questions.problem:
The function $p(x)$ is defined as

$$
p(x)=\{\begin{aligned}k+10, & \,x\le 3, \\ g(x), & \,x>3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Find the value of the constant $k$ that makes $p(x)$ continuous at $x=3.$

$k\,=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We have the piecewise function

$$
p(x)=\{\begin{aligned}k+10, & \,x\le 3, \\ 8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}, & \,x>3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

At $x=3,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}p(x) & =p(3) \\  & =k+10,\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}p(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}(8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}) \\  & =8(3)-\frac{2}{3}(3)^{3} \\  & =24-18 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
The function $p(x)$ is defined as

$$
p(x)=\{\begin{aligned}k+10, & \,x\le 3, \\ g(x), & \,x>3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Find the value of the constant $k$ that makes $p(x)$ continuous at $x=3.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $k\,=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
We have the piecewise function

$$
p(x)=\{\begin{aligned}k+10, & \,x\le 3, \\ 8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}, & \,x>3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

At $x=3,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}p(x) & =p(3) \\  & =k+10,\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}p(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}(8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}) \\  & =8(3)-\frac{2}{3}(3)^{3} \\  & =24-18 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $p(x)$ to be continuous at $x=3,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}p(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}p(x) \\ k+10 & =6 \\ k & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p(x)$ is continuous at $x=3$ when $k=-4.$

question.worked_solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Recall that $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}$ and $h(x)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x})=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}+h\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\  & =-2{e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi $ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi } & =-2{e}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ) \\  & =-2{e}^{\pi }(-1+0) \\  & =2{e}^{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $2{e}^{\pi }.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Find $det({A}^{-1})$, if $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}.
$$

First, we find $det(A):$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =-6-4 \\  & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Find $det({A}^{-1}),$ if $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}.
$$

First, we find $det(A):$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =20+2 \\  & =22\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}=\frac{1}{22}.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Find
$|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 91 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 91 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =0+1(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 92 & 93\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(3\cdot 93-6\cdot 92) \\  & =-(279-552) \\  & =273\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}.
$$

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $2$nd row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -4 & 6\end{aligned}|+1(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}-5 & 4 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}|+2(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(-18+16)+(-30-4)-2(20+3) \\  & =-4-34-46 \\  & =-84\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}=-\frac{1}{84}.
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Given that 
$|\begin{aligned}a+5 & 5 \\ b & -3\end{aligned}|=-34$,
find 
$|\begin{aligned}a+4 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}|.$
questions.worked_solution:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a+4 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}(a+5)-1 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}(a+5)-1 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}| & ={{|\begin{aligned}a+5 & 5 \\ b & -3\end{aligned}|}_{⏟}}_{-34}+|\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-34+(3-10) \\  & =-41.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 91 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =0+1(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 92 & 93\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(3\cdot 93-6\cdot 92) \\  & =-(279-552) \\  & =273\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Find $det({A}^{-1})$, if $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}.
$$

First, we find $det(A):$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =-6-4 \\  & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

det(A−1)=1det(A).

det(A)=det[−2143]=−6−4=−10

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Find $det({A}^{-1})$, if $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}.
$$

First, we find $det(A):$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =-6-4 \\  & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
det({A}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(A)}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Find
$|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 91 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|.$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 91 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =0+1(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 92 & 93\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(3\cdot 93-6\cdot 92) \\  & =-(279-552) \\  & =273\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
Find
$|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 91 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 91 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =0+1(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 92 & 93\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(3\cdot 93-6\cdot 92) \\  & =-(279-552) \\  & =273\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}.
$$

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $2$nd row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -4 & 6\end{aligned}|+1(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}-5 & 4 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}|+2(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(-18+16)+(-30-4)-2(20+3) \\  & =-4-34-46 \\  & =-84\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}=-\frac{1}{84}.
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Given that 
$|\begin{aligned}a+5 & 5 \\ b & -3\end{aligned}|=-34$,
find 
$|\begin{aligned}a+4 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}|.$
question.worked_solution:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a+4 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}(a+5)-1 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}(a+5)-1 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}| & ={{|\begin{aligned}a+5 & 5 \\ b & -3\end{aligned}|}_{⏟}}_{-34}+|\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-34+(3-10) \\  & =-41.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that |a+55b−3|=−34, find |a+45b+2−3|.

a
 39
b
 33
c
 −41
d
 43
e
 −24
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

|a+45b+2−3|=|(a+5)−15b+2−3|

Now, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

|(a+5)−15b+2−3|=|a+55b−3|⏟−34+|−152−3|=−34+(3−10)=−41.

solution.reasoning: The given determinant is -3(a+5)-5b=-34. The requested determinant is -3(a+4)-5(b+2), which differs by 3-10=-7. Its value is therefore -34-7=-41, option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem:

find 
$|\begin{aligned}a+4 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}|.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a+4 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}(a+5)-1 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}(a+5)-1 & 5 \\ b+2 & -3\end{aligned}| & ={{|\begin{aligned}a+5 & 5 \\ b & -3\end{aligned}|}_{⏟}}_{-34}+|\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-34+(3-10) \\  & =-41.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: What is the center of the hyperbola $\frac{{y}^{2}}{5}-\frac{(x+7)^{2}}{6}=1?$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

Note that the given equation can be rewritten as follows:

$$
\frac{(y-0)^{2}}{5}-\frac{(x-(-7))^{2}}{6}=1
$$

In this case, we have $h=-7$ and $k=0.$

Therefore, the center of the hyperbola is $(-7,0).$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
What is the center of the hyperbola 
$-2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+12x=22?$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in the above form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+12x & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2{x}^{2}+12x & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2[{x}^{2}-6x] & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2[(x-3)^{2}-9] & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2(x-3)^{2}+18 & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2(x-3)^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the center is $(3,0).$

questions.problem:
The center of the hyperbola ${x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-10x-16y=-5$ is$\,\,($
{{field-1}}$,$

questions.worked_solution:
The equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in standard form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-10x-16y & =-5 \\ ({x}^{2}-10x)-4({y}^{2}+4y) & =-5 \\ [(x-5)^{2}-25]-4[(y+2)^{2}-4] & =-5 \\ (x-5)^{2}-25-4(y+2)^{2}+16 & =-5 \\ (x-5)^{2}-4(y+2)^{2} & =-5+25-16 \\ (x-5)^{2}-4(y+2)^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{{2}^{2}}-\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{{1}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{{2}^{2}}-\frac{(y-(-2))^{2}}{{1}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the center of the hyperbola is $(\,5,-2\,).$

question.problem:
What is the center of the hyperbola 
$-2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+12x=22?$
question.worked_solution:
The equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in the above form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+12x & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2{x}^{2}+12x & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2[{x}^{2}-6x] & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2[(x-3)^{2}-9] & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2(x-3)^{2}+18 & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2(x-3)^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
The equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in the above form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+12x & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2{x}^{2}+12x & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2[{x}^{2}-6x] & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2[(x-3)^{2}-9] & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2(x-3)^{2}+18 & =22 \\ {y}^{2}-2(x-3)^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the center is $(3,0).$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Calculate $F(x)$ given that $f(x)={x}^{13}$ and ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=13$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{13}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{13+1}}{13+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{14})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\cdot 14\,{x}^{13} & = \\ {x}^{13}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Calculate $F(x)$ given that $f(x)={x}^{4}$ and ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=4$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4+1}}{4+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{5}\cdot 5{x}^{4} & = \\ {x}^{4}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Calculate $\int {x}^{20}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the power rule with $n=20$, and we get

$$
\int {x}^{20}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{20+1}}{20+1}+C=\frac{{x}^{21}}{21}+C.
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{21}}{21}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{21}}{21})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{21}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{21})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{21}\cdot 21{x}^{20} & = \\ {x}^{20}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: $\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{1}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{1/2+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{3/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt{{x}^{3}}={x}^{3/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2+1}}{(\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5/2}}{(\frac{5}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\cdot \frac{5}{2}{x}^{5/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{3/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{3/2}}$ and that ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{{x}^{3/2}}={x}^{-3/2}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3/2+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/2}}{(-\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =-2{x}^{-1/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{{x}^{1/2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Given that $f(x)={x}^{-1/7}$ and that ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{1}{7}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-1/7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/7+1}}{(-\frac{1}{7}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6/7}}{(\frac{6}{7})}+C \\  & =\frac{7}{6}{x}^{6/7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}$ and that ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}={x}^{-3/2}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3/2+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/2}}{(-\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =-2{x}^{-1/2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Antiderivative of a Monomial
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int x^2 \,\textrm d x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We apply the power rule with $n=2$, and we get

$$
\int x^2 \,\textrm d x = \dfrac{x^{2+1}}{2+1} + C = \dfrac{x^3}{3}+C.
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{3}\cdot 3{x}^{2} & = \\ {x}^{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Antiderivative of a Radical Function
canonical_examples.problem: Find the antiderivative of  $\sqrt x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start by writing the square root as a rational power, $\sqrt x= x^{1/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{1/2+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{3/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

                    Finding the Antiderivative of a Reciprocal Function
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $f(x) = \dfrac 1 {x^3}$ and that $F'(x) = f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if $F'(x) = f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\dfrac 1 {x^3}= x^{-3}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-3$ and get

tutorials.problem:
An **antiderivative** is the *opposite* of a derivative. For example:

- Using the power rule, we know that the *derivative* of $\color{blue}x^2$ is ${\color{red}2x}.$

- Going in the *opposite* direction, we say that an **antiderivative** of $\color{red}2x$ is ${\color{blue}x^2}.$

For any given function, there are infinitely many antiderivatives. For example:

- The derivative of $\color{blue}x^2$ is ${\color{red}2x},$ so an *antiderivative* of $\color{red}2x$ is ${\color{blue}x^2}.$

- The derivative of $\color{blue}x^2+1$ is ${\color{red}2x},$ so another *antiderivative* of $\color{red}2x$ is ${\color{blue}x^2+1}.$

- The derivative of $\color{blue}x^2+2$ is ${\color{red}2x},$ so another *antiderivative* of $\color{red}2x$ is ${\color{blue}x^2+2}.$

- ...

In general, all the antiderivatives of $\color{red}2x$ can be written in the form ${\color{blue}x^2+C},$ where $C$ is a constant.

To represent the antiderivative symbolically, we use a special symbol $\displaystyle \int$ called the **integral** symbol. So, using **integral notation**, we can write

$$
\int 2x \, \textrm d x = x^2 + C
$$

where $C$ represents an arbitrary constant and is called the **constant of integration**.

In words, $\displaystyle \int 2x \, \textrm d x$ is said as “the integral of $2x$ with respect to $x$” or “the antiderivative of $2x$.” Integrals like this are called **indefinite integrals**, and the function being **integrated** ($2x$ in this case) is called the **integrand**.

tutorials.name: The Power Rule for Integration
tutorials.problem:
To compute the integral of any power function $x^n,$ where $n \neq -1,$ we can use the **power rule for integration**. The power rule for integration states that

$$
\int x^n\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac {x^{n + 1}}{n + 1} + C,
$$

where $C$ is any constant and $n\neq -1.$ For example, in the case of $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{3+1}}{3+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So the **antiderivative** of $f'(x) = x^3$ is $f(x) = \dfrac {x^{4}}{4}+C .$ 

We can check that this is the correct answer by taking the derivative of $f(x)$ and seeing that it is indeed equal to $x^3\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{4}(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{x}^{4})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{4}\cdot 4{x}^{4-1} & = \\ {x}^{3}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the constant $C$ disappeared when we differentiated because the derivative of any constant is zero. We always add $+C$ whenever we find the antiderivative of a function because we know that it will disappear when we differentiate.

**Note:** The power rule for integration is just the power rule for differentiation in reverse!

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left( x^{n+1} \right) = (n+1)x^n \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \displaystyle \int x^n \, \textrm dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}
$$

tutorials.name: Some Final Notes on Indefinite Integrals and Constants
tutorials.problem:
Let's recap the main points:

- Integrals like $\displaystyle \int x^3\,\textrm d x$ are called **indefinite integrals**.

- Whenever we calculate an indefinite integral, we must always remember to add an **arbitrary constant** $+C.$

- To integrate power functions, we can use the **power rule for integration**, which states that

$$
\int x^n\,\textrm d x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C,
$$

provided that $n \neq -1.$ To emphasize, the power rule does *not* work when $n=-1.$ So we cannot use the above formula to work out $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{x}\,\textrm d x.$ Integrals like this need to be handled differently, and you'll find out how soon.

observed_steps.name: Example: Finding the Antiderivative of a Monomial
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We apply the power rule with $n=2$, and we get

$$
\int x^2 \,\textrm d x = \dfrac{x^{2+1}}{2+1} + C = \dfrac{x^3}{3}+C.
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{3}\cdot 3{x}^{2} & = \\ {x}^{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$

$$

Question 1
?

Calculate F(x) given that f(x)=x13 and F′(x)=f(x).

a
x14+C
b
x1212+C
c
x1414+C
d
13x14+C
e
x1213+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

We apply the power rule with n=13, and we get

F(x)=∫f(x)dx=∫x13dx=x13+113+1+C=x1414+C. Let's check by differentiating:

ddx(x1414+C)=ddx(x1414)+ddx(C)=114ddx(x14)+0=114⋅14x13=x13✓

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Antiderivative of a Monomial
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=4$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4+1}}{4+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{5}\cdot 5{x}^{4} & = \\ {x}^{4}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=4$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4+1}}{4+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}

$$

a

x2121+C

Correct

We apply the power rule with n=20, and we get

∫x20dx=x20+120+1+C=x2121+C.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We start by writing the square root as a rational power, $\sqrt x= x^{1/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{1/2+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{3/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2+1}}{(\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5/2}}{(\frac{5}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\cdot \frac{5}{2}{x}^{5/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{3/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Radical Function

observed_steps.name: Example: Finding the Antiderivative of a Reciprocal Function
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Antiderivative of a Radical Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if $F'(x) = f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\dfrac 1 {x^3}= x^{-3}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-3$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3+1}}{-3+1}+C \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{-2}}{2}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Given that f(x)=1x3/2 and that F′(x)=f(x), calculate F(x).

a
x1/2+C
b
1x1/2+C
c
−52x5/2+C
d
−2x1/2+C
e
−2x5/2+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

Note that 1x3/2=x−3/2. So, we can use the power rule with n=−32 and get F(x)=∫f(x)dx=∫x−3/2dx=x−3/2+1(−32+1)+C=x−1/2(−12)+C=−2x−1/2+C=−2x1/2+C.

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Antiderivative of a Reciprocal Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{1}{7}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-1/7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/7+1}}{(-\frac{1}{7}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6/7}}{(\frac{6}{7})}+C \\  & =\frac{7}{6}{x}^{6/7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Given that f(x)=x−1/7 and that F′(x)=f(x), calculate F(x).

a
76x6/7+C
b
16x1/7+C
c
−16x6/7+C
d
−76x5/7+C
e
56x−6/7+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

We can use the power rule with n=−17 and get F(x)=∫f(x)dx=∫x−1/7dx=x−1/7+1(−17+1)+C=x6/7(67)+C=76x6/7+C.

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Antiderivative of a Reciprocal Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}={x}^{-3/2}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3/2+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/2}}{(-\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =-2{x}^{-1/2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}={x}^{-3/2}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3/2+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/2}}{(-\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =-2{x}^{-1/2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that f(x)=1x3 and that F′(x)=f(x), calculate F(x).

a
−3x3/2+C
b
x−3/2+C
c
2x1/2+C
d
x−1/3+C
e
−2x−1/2+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

Note that 1x3=x−3/2. So, we can use the power rule with n=−32 and get

F(x)=∫1x3dx=∫x−3/2dx=x−3/2+1(−32+1)+C=x−1/2(−12)+C=−2x−1/2+C.

tutorial.name: Some Final Notes on Indefinite Integrals and Constants
tutorial.problem:
Let's recap the main points:

- Integrals like $\displaystyle \int x^3\,\textrm d x$ are called **indefinite integrals**.

- Whenever we calculate an indefinite integral, we must always remember to add an **arbitrary constant** $+C.$

- To integrate power functions, we can use the **power rule for integration**, which states that

$$
\int x^n\,\textrm d x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C,
$$

provided that $n \neq -1.$ To emphasize, the power rule does *not* work when $n=-1.$ So we cannot use the above formula to work out $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{x}\,\textrm d x.$ Integrals like this need to be handled differently, and you'll find out how soon.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Calculate $F(x)$ given that $f(x)={x}^{13}$ and ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x).$
question.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=13$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{13}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{13+1}}{13+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{14})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\cdot 14\,{x}^{13} & = \\ {x}^{13}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=13$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{13}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{13+1}}{13+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{14})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\cdot 14\,{x}^{13} & = \\ {x}^{13}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate F(x) given that f(x)=x13 and F′(x)=f(x).

a
x14+C
b
x1212+C

x1414+C

13x14+C

EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

We apply the power rule with n=13, and we get

F(x)=∫f(x)dx=∫x13dx=x13+113+1+C=x1414+C. Let's check by differentiating:

ddx(x1414+C)=ddx(x1414)+ddx(C)=114ddx(x14)+0=114⋅14x13=x13✓

Question 1
?

Calculate F(x) given that f(x)=x13 and F′(x)=f(x).

a
x14+C
b
x1212+C
c
x1414+C
d
13x14+C
e
x1213+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

We apply the power rule with n=13, and we get

F(x)=∫f(x)dx=∫x13dx=x13+113+1+C=x1414+C. Let's check by differentiating:

ddx(x1414+C)=ddx(x1414)+ddx(C)=114ddx(x14)+0=114⋅14x13=x13✓

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Calculate $F(x)$ given that $f(x)={x}^{4}$ and ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x).$
question.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=4$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4+1}}{4+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{5}\cdot 5{x}^{4} & = \\ {x}^{4}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Calculate F(x) given that f(x)=x4 and F′(x)=f(x).

a
x44+C
b
x55+C
c
x45+C
d
4x5+C
e
5x5+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

We apply the power rule with n=4, and we get

F(x)=∫f(x)dx=∫x4dx=x4+14+1+C=x55+C. Let's check by differentiating:

ddx(x55+C)=ddx(x55)+ddx(C)=15ddx(x5)+0=15⋅5x4=x4✓

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Antiderivative of a Monomial
last_observation.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=4$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4+1}}{4+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{5}\cdot 5{x}^{4} & = \\ {x}^{4}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Calculate F(x) given that f(x)=x4 and F′(x)=f(x).

a
x44+C
b
x55+C
c
x45+C
d
4x5+C
e
5x5+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

We apply the power rule with n=4, and we get

F(x)=∫f(x)dx=∫x4dx=x4+14+1+C=x55+C. Let's check by differentiating:

ddx(x55+C)=ddx(x55)+ddx(C)=15ddx(x5)+0=15⋅5x4=x4✓

solution.reasoning: The antiderivative power rule gives F(x)=x^5/5+C. Its derivative is (5/5)x^4=x^4, so option b is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes the key for this question; the supplied worked example addresses x^2.

Question 2
?

Calculate F(x) given that f(x)=x4 and F′(x)=f(x).

a
x44+C
b
x55+C
c
x45+C
d
4x5+C
e
5x5+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

We apply the power rule with n=4, and we get

F(x)=∫f(x)dx=∫x4dx=x4+14+1+C=x55+C. Let's check by differentiating:

ddx(x55+C)=ddx(x55)+ddx(C)=15ddx(x5)+0=15⋅5x4=x4✓

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Calculate $\int {x}^{20}\,\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
We apply the power rule with $n=20$, and we get

$$
\int {x}^{20}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{20+1}}{20+1}+C=\frac{{x}^{21}}{21}+C.
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{21}}{21}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{21}}{21})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{21}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{21})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{21}\cdot 21{x}^{20} & = \\ {x}^{20}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Calculate $\int {x}^{20}\,\text{d}x.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We apply the power rule with $n=20$, and we get

$$
\int {x}^{20}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{20+1}}{20+1}+C=\frac{{x}^{21}}{21}+C.

$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: $\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{1}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{1/2+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{3/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

∫xdx=

a
2x5/25+C
b
2x3/23+C
c
2x1/23+C
d
x1/22+C
e
x3/22+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start by writing the root as a rational power, x=x1/2. So, we can apply the power rule with n=12 and get

∫xdx=∫x1/2dx=x1/2+1(12+1)+C=x3/2(32)+C=2x3/23+C.

Again, let's check by differentiating:

ddx(2x3/23+C)=ddx(2x3/23)+ddx(C)=23ddx(x3/2)+0=23⋅32x3/2−1=x1/2✓

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Antiderivative of a Radical Function
last_observation.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{1}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{1/2+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{3/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: $\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{1}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{1/2+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We start by writing the root as a rational power, x=x1/2. So, we can apply the power rule with n=12 and get

∫xdx=∫x1/2dx=x1/2+1(12+1)+C=x3/2(32)+C=2x3/23+C.

ddx(2x3/23+C)=ddx(2x3/23)+ddx(C)=23ddx(x3/2)+0=23⋅32x3/2−1=x1/2✓

solution.reasoning: Write √x as x^{1/2}. The power rule gives x^{3/2}/(3/2)+C=2x^{3/2}/3+C, whose derivative is √x. Option b matches the captured Math Academy worked solution for this same integral.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: $\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x=$
feedback.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{1}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{1/2+1}}{(\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{3/2}}{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{3/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{1/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: $\int \sqrt{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt{{x}^{3}}={x}^{3/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2+1}}{(\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5/2}}{(\frac{5}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\cdot \frac{5}{2}{x}^{5/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{3/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Antiderivative of a Radical Function
last_observation.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt{{x}^{3}}={x}^{3/2}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/2+1}}{(\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5/2}}{(\frac{5}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2{x}^{5/2}}{5})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/2})+0 & = \\ \frac{2}{5}\cdot \frac{5}{2}{x}^{5/2-1} & = \\ {x}^{3/2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

∫x3dx=

a
25x5/2+C
b
37x3/2+C
c
113x5/2+C
d
115x3/2+C
e
175x5/2+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start by writing the root as a rational power, x3=x3/2. So, we can apply the power rule with n=32 and get ∫x3dx=∫x3/2dx=x3/2+1(32+1)+C=x5/2(52)+C=2x5/25+C.

Again, let's check by differentiating:

ddx(2x5/25+C)=ddx(2x5/25)+ddx(C)=25ddx(x5/2)+0=25⋅52x5/2−1=x3/2✓
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Radical Function

solution.reasoning: For real x≥0, √(x^3)=x^{3/2}. The power rule gives x^{5/2}/(5/2)+C=(2/5)x^{5/2}+C, whose derivative is x^{3/2}. Therefore option a is mathematically correct. The captured worked example concerns √x, so it does not establish Math Academy's answer to this question.

EXPLANATION

We start by writing the root as a rational power, x3=x3/2. So, we can apply the power rule with n=32 and get ∫x3dx=∫x3/2dx=x3/2+1(32+1)+C=x5/2(52)+C=2x5/25+C.

Again, let's check by differentiating:

ddx(2x5/25+C)=ddx(2x5/25)+ddx(C)=25ddx(x5/2)+0=25⋅52x5/2−1=x3/2✓

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Given that $f(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{3/2}}$ and that ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$
question.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{{x}^{3/2}}={x}^{-3/2}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3/2+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/2}}{(-\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =-2{x}^{-1/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{{x}^{1/2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Given that f(x)=1x3/2 and that F′(x)=f(x), calculate F(x).

a
x1/2+C
b
1x1/2+C
c
−52x5/2+C
d
−2x1/2+C
e
−2x5/2+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{{x}^{3/2}}={x}^{-3/2}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3/2+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/2}}{(-\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =-2{x}^{-1/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{{x}^{1/2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

b

EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

Note that 1x3/2=x−3/2. So, we can use the power rule with n=−32 and get F(x)=∫f(x)dx=∫x−3/2dx=x−3/2+1(−32+1)+C=x−1/2(−12)+C=−2x−1/2+C=−2x1/2+C.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Reciprocal Function

solution.reasoning: For x>0, f(x)=x^{-3/2}. The antiderivative power rule gives F(x)=x^{-1/2}/(-1/2)+C=-2/x^{1/2}+C, whose derivative is x^{-3/2}. Thus option d is mathematically correct. The captured example integrates x^{-3}, so it does not establish Math Academy's answer for this question.

question.name: Question 7
question.problem: Given that $f(x)={x}^{-1/7}$ and that ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$
question.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{1}{7}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-1/7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/7+1}}{(-\frac{1}{7}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6/7}}{(\frac{6}{7})}+C \\  & =\frac{7}{6}{x}^{6/7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Antiderivative of a Reciprocal Function
last_observation.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{1}{7}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-1/7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/7+1}}{(-\frac{1}{7}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6/7}}{(\frac{6}{7})}+C \\  & =\frac{7}{6}{x}^{6/7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Given that f(x)=x−1/7 and that F′(x)=f(x), calculate F(x).

a
76x6/7+C
b
16x1/7+C
c
−16x6/7+C
d
−76x5/7+C
e
56x−6/7+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

We can use the power rule with n=−17 and get F(x)=∫f(x)dx=∫x−1/7dx=x−1/7+1(−17+1)+C=x6/7(67)+C=76x6/7+C.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Reciprocal Function

solution.reasoning: The antiderivative power rule gives F(x)=x^{6/7}/(6/7)+C=(7/6)x^{6/7}+C. Differentiating yields (7/6)(6/7)x^{-1/7}=x^{-1/7}, so option a is mathematically correct. The captured example integrates x^{-3}; no supplied Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key.

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem: Given that $f(x)={x}^{-1/7}$ and that ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{1}{7}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-1/7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/7+1}}{(-\frac{1}{7}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6/7}}{(\frac{6}{7})}+C \\  & =\frac{7}{6}{x}^{6/7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem: Given that $f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}$ and that ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$
question.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}={x}^{-3/2}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{3}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-3/2+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/2}}{(-\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =-2{x}^{-1/2}+C.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 8
?

Given that f(x)=1x3 and that F′(x)=f(x), calculate F(x).

a
−3x3/2+C
b
x−3/2+C
c
2x1/2+C
d
x−1/3+C
e
−2x−1/2+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if F′(x)=f(x), then integrating both sides of this equation gives

F′(x)=f(x)∫F′(x)dx=∫f(x)dxF(x)=∫f(x)dx.

Note that 1x3=x−3/2. So, we can use the power rule with n=−32 and get

F(x)=∫1x3dx=∫x−3/2dx=x−3/2+1(−32+1)+C=x−1/2(−12)+C=−2x−1/2+C.
